faq.a: Both mean yes. 응 is casual, for friends and younger people. 네 is polite, for elders and strangers.

faq.q: Is it rude to say eung to older people?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Unless you are very close, say 네 to anyone older than you.

faq.q: What does ㅇㅇ mean?
faq.a: ㅇㅇ is the texting shorthand for 응, so it means "yeah" or "ok".

intro: 정말 (jeongmal) means "really" or "truly". Said alone as a question, 정말? means "Really?", and before a word it adds emphasis, as in 정말 고마워 ("Thank you so much").
literal: 정말 is commonly traced to 정 (正, "correct" or "true") plus 말 ("words"), so it is close to "true words".
usage: 정말 works almost like 진짜 (jinjja). Both mean "really", but 정말 sounds a little more standard and is slightly more natural in polite speech and writing.
As a question, 정말? is casual and 정말요? is polite. As an intensifier, 정말 fits any level: 정말 감사합니다 is perfectly respectful.
Do not overuse it in every sentence. Like "really" in English, it loses force if it appears everywhere.

examples.context: Hearing good news from a coworker
Thanking a friend who helped you move
Complimenting food at a restaurant

faq.q: What is the difference between jeongmal and jinjja?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. 진짜 is a bit more casual and common in speech, while 정말 sounds a little more standard and polite.

faq.q: Is jeongmal polite?
faq.a: 정말 itself is neutral. Add 요 for the polite question 정말요?, and use it freely in phrases like 정말 감사합니다.

faq.q: How do you say "really?" politely in Korean?
faq.a: Say 정말요? or 진짜요?. 정말요? sounds slightly more polished.

meaning: Oh no, we're in big trouble!
intro: 큰일 났어 (keunil nasseo) means "Oh no, I'm in big trouble!" or "Something terrible happened!". People say it the moment they realize something has gone badly wrong.
literal: 큰 means "big" and 일 means "matter" or "thing", so 큰일 is "a big problem". 났어 is the past tense of 나다, "to happen" or "to break out". Together: "A big problem has happened."
usage: Say 큰일 났어 when you suddenly realize a disaster: you forgot an exam, broke something, or are very late. It is often said in a panic, and the next line is usually 어떡해 ("What do I do?").
큰일 났다 is very common too, especially when talking to yourself. With people you should be polite to, say 큰일 났어요.
It is also used for mild, playful "disasters", like realizing you ate the whole cake. The spacing 큰일 났어 is standard, but many people type it as 큰일났어.

forms.note: Plain form, often said to yourself.

examples.context: Looking at the clock after oversleeping
A child runs to tell their mom something
Remembering the exam is tomorrow
examples.en: Oh no, the exam is tomorrow

faq.q: What does keunil nasseo mean?
faq.a: 큰일 났어 means "Something terrible happened" or "I'm in big trouble". It is a panicked reaction to a sudden problem.

faq.q: Is it keunil nasseo or keunillasseo?
faq.a: It is written 큰일 났어. When spoken, the sounds blend, so it can sound like "keunil-lasseo".

faq.q: Can I say keunil nasseo to my boss?
faq.a: Use the polite 큰일 났어요 with a boss or anyone older.

intro: 아니 (ani) means "No" in casual Korean. It is also used at the start of a sentence like "Wait" or "I mean", to show surprise, disbelief or to correct yourself.
literal: 아니 is related to 아니다, "to not be". The polite answer is 아니요, often shortened to 아뇨.
usage: Use 아니 to answer no to friends, siblings and younger people. With elders or strangers, say 아니요.
Koreans also start sentences with 아니 when they are surprised or frustrated, like "Wait, what?" or "No, but seriously". For example, 아니 진짜? means "Wait, really?"
Be careful with tone. A sharp 아니! can sound like you are snapping at someone, while a soft 아니~ is gentle.

forms.note: Polite form for elders and strangers.
Short, natural spoken form of 아니요.

examples.context: A friend asks if you are upset
Hearing shocking gossip
Turning down a snack

faq.q: What is the difference between ani and aniyo?
faq.a: Both mean no. 아니 is casual and 아니요 (or 아뇨) is polite.

faq.q: Why do Koreans say ani at the start of a sentence?
faq.a: Here 아니 works like "Wait" or "I mean". It shows surprise, frustration or a change of thought, not a literal no.

faq.q: Is ani rude?
faq.a: Not by itself, but it is casual. Say 아니요 to anyone older.

intro: 그럼 (geureom) means "Of course!" when you answer someone, and "Then" or "In that case" at the start of a sentence. Both uses are very common in everyday Korean.
literal: 그럼 is a shortened form of 그러면, "if so" or "then". The "of course" meaning grew from that: "If you ask, then naturally."
usage: As an answer, 그럼! is a warm, confident "Of course!" With people you should be polite to, say 그럼요!
At the start of a sentence, 그럼 means "then" or "so": 그럼 내일 봐 ("Then see you tomorrow"). This 그럼 is fine in casual talk, and you can follow it with a polite sentence when speaking to elders.
그럼 그렇지 means "I knew it" or "Of course that happened", often said with a sigh.

forms.note: Used to wrap up a talk or message.

examples.context: A friend asks if you will come to their party
Making plans at the end of a call
Your teacher asks if you did your homework

faq.q: What does geureom mean in Korean?
faq.a: 그럼 means "of course" as an answer, and "then" or "in that case" at the start of a sentence.

faq.q: Is geureom polite?
faq.a: As a one-word answer it is casual. Say 그럼요 to be polite.

faq.q: What is the difference between geureom and geureomyeon?
faq.a: 그럼 is the short form of 그러면. In speech, 그럼 is far more common.

intro: 야 (ya) means "Hey!" in Korean. It is a casual way to get someone's attention or call out to them, and in K-dramas it is often shouted in anger or surprise.
literal: 야 is an interjection. A related ending, 야 or 아, is also added to first names to call someone, as in 민수야 ("Minsu!").
usage: Use 야 only with close friends, younger siblings and people younger than you. Saying 야 to an older person or a stranger is very rude and can start a fight.
It can be friendly, like "Hey, look at this", or angry, like "Hey! What are you doing?" The tone does all the work.
To call a name casually, add 야 after a name ending in a vowel (지수야) and 아 after a consonant (민준아). To get a stranger's attention politely, say 저기요 instead.

forms.note: Shouted to get attention or show anger.
Casual, for friends and younger people: 지수야, 민준아.
Polite way to get a stranger's attention.

examples.context: Waking up your younger brother
Showing a friend a funny video
Calling a close friend to dinner

faq.q: Is saying ya rude in Korean?
faq.a: It can be. 야 is fine with close friends and younger people, but it is very rude to say to elders, bosses or strangers.

faq.q: Why do Koreans add ya to names?
faq.a: Adding 야 or 아 to a first name is the casual way to call someone, like 지수야. It is used with friends and younger people.

faq.q: How do I get a stranger's attention politely?
faq.a: Say 저기요, which works like "Excuse me".

intro: 됐어 (dwaesseo) means "Forget it", "Never mind" or "That's enough". It can also mean "It's done" or "It worked", and said sharply it shuts a conversation down.
literal: 됐어 is the past tense of 되다, "to become" or "to be done", with a casual ending. Literally it is close to "It's done" or "That will do".
usage: The most common use is refusing or ending something: 됐어, 내가 할게 ("Forget it, I'll do it myself"). Said coldly, it is like "Whatever, forget it" and can hurt feelings, especially in an argument.
It is also positive: when something finally works or is finished, people say 됐다! or 됐어!, like "Got it!" or "Done!"
With people you should be polite to, 됐어요 is a common way to decline something, like "No thanks, I'm fine". Even so, a soft tone matters, because 됐어요 said flatly sounds cold.

forms.note: Often said with relief or joy.

examples.context: Your friend keeps offering to help, too late
Finally fixing your laptop
Declining a shop's plastic bag

faq.q: Is dwaesseo rude?
faq.a: It depends on the tone. Said sharply in an argument it is dismissive, like "Forget it". Said with relief, it just means "Done!"

faq.q: What does dwaesseoyo mean?
faq.a: 됐어요 is the polite form. It is often used to decline, like "No thanks, I'm fine".

faq.q: What is the difference between dwaesseo and gwaenchana?
faq.a: Both can decline an offer. 괜찮아 sounds gentle ("I'm okay"), while 됐어 is blunter and can sound like "Forget it".

intro: 깜짝이야 (kkamjjagiya) means "You scared me!" or "That startled me!". People say it the moment something makes them jump, like a friend sneaking up or a loud noise.
literal: 깜짝 is a word for being startled, as in 깜짝 놀라다 ("to be startled"). 이야 turns it into an exclamation, a bit like "What a fright!"
usage: Say 깜짝이야 right after you get a fright. It is often paired with 아 or 아이고: 아 깜짝이야! is extremely common.
It is an exclamation about how you feel, not something said at a person, so it is fine around anyone, including elders. If you want to tell an older person they startled you, say 깜짝 놀랐어요.
It is also used half jokingly, when someone appears suddenly or says something surprising.

examples.context: A friend taps your shoulder from behind
Your roommate is suddenly standing in the kitchen
examples.en: You scared me! When did you get here?

examples.context: Your sibling bursts into your room

faq.q: Is kkamjjagiya rude?
faq.a: No. It describes your own reaction, so you can say it around anyone.

faq.q: What does a kkamjjagiya mean?
faq.a: 아 깜짝이야 means "Oh, you scared me!". The 아 is just a gasp of surprise.

faq.q: What is the difference between kkamjjagiya and eomma-ya?
faq.a: Both are reactions to a fright. 엄마야 is more of a sudden cry, like "Eek!", while 깜짝이야 means "That startled me!".

intro: 싫어 (sireo) means "No!", "I don't want to" or "I hate it". It is a direct, casual way to refuse something or say you dislike it.
literal: 싫어 comes from the adjective 싫다, "to be disliked" or "to be unwanted". The ㅎ in the spelling 싫어 is silent, so it sounds like "shi-reo".
usage: Use 싫어 to refuse an offer or plan ("No, I don't want to") or to say you dislike something: 오이 싫어 ("I hate cucumbers").

It is casual and blunt. It is fine with friends and family, and in K-dramas a playful 싫어~ is a classic teasing line between couples. With elders, a flat 싫어요 can sound rude, so softer phrases like 괜찮아요 ("I'm okay") are safer for refusing.
Grammar tip: 싫다 describes something as disliked, while 싫어하다 is the verb "to dislike", used for describing other people: 그는 오이를 싫어해 ("He dislikes cucumbers").

forms.note: Verb form, often about other people.

examples.context: A friend wants to go hiking in the rain
examples.en: No, I don't want to go

examples.context: Picking cucumbers out of your gimbap
A child refusing to go to bed

faq.q: Is sireo rude?
faq.a: It is blunt but not offensive with friends and family. With elders, a direct 싫어요 can sound rude, so use a softer refusal.

faq.q: What is the difference between sireo and sireohae?
faq.a: 싫어 is how you say you yourself dislike or refuse something. 싫어해 is usually used to describe what someone else dislikes.

faq.q: How do you pronounce sireo?
faq.a: It sounds like "shi-reo". The ㅎ in 싫어 is silent.

intro: 맞아 (maja) means "Right!", "Exactly" or "That's true". It is the casual way to agree with what someone just said.
literal: 맞아 comes from 맞다, "to be correct" or "to be right", with a casual ending.
usage: Say 맞아 when you agree with a friend. Doubling it, 맞아 맞아, is a very natural, enthusiastic "Yes, exactly!"
With people you should be polite to, say 맞아요, and in formal settings 맞습니다.
A related favorite is 아 맞다!, "Oh, right!", said when you suddenly remember something you forgot.

forms.note: Said when you suddenly remember something.

examples.context: A friend says the new café is too expensive
Your friend guesses the answer
Agreeing with a coworker

faq.q: What does maja maja mean?
faq.a: 맞아 맞아 means "Right, right!" or "Exactly!". It is enthusiastic agreement.

faq.q: Is maja polite?
faq.a: No, it is casual. Say 맞아요 or, more formally, 맞습니다.

faq.q: What does a matda mean?
faq.a: 아 맞다 means "Oh, right!". People say it when they suddenly remember something.

intro: 그치 (geuchi) means "Right?" or "Isn't it?" when you ask for agreement, and "Right" or "I know" when you agree. It is a relaxed, friendly word used all the time between friends.
literal: 그치 is a spoken contraction of 그렇지, which comes from 그렇다 ("to be so") plus the ending 지 that seeks or confirms agreement.
usage: Add 그치? to the end of a statement to ask "right?": 맛있지, 그치? ("It's good, right?"). Said on its own as a reply, 그치 means "Right" or "I know, right?"
It is casual and a little soft or cute, common among friends, couples and in texts. With people you should be polite to, use 그렇죠 or the more relaxed 그쵸.
Compared with 맞아, 그치 sounds warmer and more like you are sharing a feeling.

examples.context: Sharing dessert with a friend
Agreeing with a friend's opinion
Walking outside in summer

faq.q: What does geuchi mean?
faq.a: 그치 means "Right?" when asking for agreement, or "Right" when agreeing. It comes from 그렇지.

faq.q: Is geuchi polite?
faq.a: No, it is casual. Use 그렇죠 or 그쵸 with people you should be polite to.

faq.q: What is the difference between geuchi and maja?
faq.a: 맞아 is a clear "That's correct". 그치 is softer and more like "I know, right?"

intro: 엄마야 (eomma-ya) is a Korean cry of fright that means "Eek!" or "Oh my gosh!". Literally it is "Mom!", and people blurt it out when something suddenly startles them.
literal: 엄마 means "mom" and 야 is the ending used when calling someone. So 엄마야 is literally calling out "Mom!", the way a startled child might.
usage: Say 엄마야 at the instant of a fright: a bug, a sudden noise, a near fall. It is a reflex, not a sentence, and is often followed by 깜짝이야.
It is casual and a little old-fashioned or comic. You hear it from people of all ages, and it is not rude, but it is a cry rather than something you say to someone.
Even though it literally calls your mom, nobody expects their mother to answer. It works the same way "Oh my gosh!" does in English.

examples.context: Someone jumps out from behind a door
Seeing a cockroach in the kitchen
Almost slipping on ice

faq.q: Why do Koreans say eomma-ya when scared?
faq.a: 엄마야 literally means "Mom!". Like a child calling for their mother, it became a reflex cry when startled.

faq.q: Is eomma-ya the same as omo?
faq.a: They are close. 어머 is general surprise, while 엄마야 is usually a stronger, more sudden fright.

faq.q: Is eomma-ya rude?
faq.a: No. It is casual and a bit comic, but it is not rude.

intro: 혹시 (hoksi) means "by any chance" or "perhaps". Koreans put it at the start of a question to make it softer and more polite, as in 혹시 시간 있어요? ("Do you have time, by any chance?").
literal: 혹시 comes from the Chinese characters 或是, which together carry the sense of "perhaps" or "possibly".
usage: 혹시 is one of the most useful softeners in Korean. Starting a question with it makes it sound careful and considerate, which is why it is common when asking strangers, coworkers or people you just met.

It fits any politeness level: add it to casual questions with friends or polite questions with elders. It is also used in K-dramas when someone nervously asks something personal, like "Do you, by any chance, like me?"
혹시나 and 혹시 모르니까 mean "just in case": 혹시 모르니까 우산 가져가 ("Take an umbrella, just in case").

forms.note: Adds a feeling of doubt or caution.

forms.en: By any chance? / Do you mean...?

examples.context: Meeting someone abroad
examples.en: Are you Korean, by any chance?

examples.context: Asking a friend to hang out
examples.en: Do you have time, by any chance?

examples.context: Your friend is unusually quiet
examples.en: Are you mad, by any chance?

faq.q: What does hoksi mean in Korean?
faq.a: 혹시 means "by any chance" or "perhaps". It softens a question and makes it sound more polite.

faq.q: Is hoksi polite?
faq.a: 혹시 is neutral, so it fits both casual and polite speech. It actually makes questions sound more considerate.

faq.q: What does hoksina mean?
faq.a: 혹시나 means "just in case" or "in the off chance", often showing a bit of worry or hope.

intro: 닥쳐 (dakchyeo) means "Shut up!" in Korean. It is a harsh, rude command and much stronger than a playful "be quiet". In K-dramas you hear it in fights and tense scenes.
literal: 닥쳐 is the casual command form of 닥치다, which in this sense means "to shut one's mouth".
usage: 닥쳐 is genuinely rude. Never say it to parents, teachers, bosses, older people or strangers. Even with friends it can cause a real argument unless you are obviously joking and very close.
입 닥쳐 ("Shut your mouth") is even stronger and more aggressive. If you just want someone to be quiet, 조용히 해 ("Be quiet") or 그만해 ("Stop it") are much milder.
Learners mostly need to understand 닥쳐 when they hear it in dramas, not use it. If you do joke with it among close friends, keep your tone clearly playful.

examples.context: Two siblings fighting in a drama scene
A close friend keeps spoiling a movie
A tense argument between rivals
examples.en: Shut up, I don't want to hear it

faq.q: Is dakchyeo a bad word?
faq.a: It is not profanity, but it is very rude. It is like a harsh "Shut up!" and should never be said to elders or strangers.

faq.q: Can I say dakchyeo to my friends?
faq.a: Only if you are very close and clearly joking. Otherwise it can start a real fight.

faq.q: What is a politer way to say be quiet in Korean?
faq.a: Say 조용히 해 to friends, or 조용히 해 주세요 to be polite.

meaning: Get it together! / Snap out of it!
intro: 정신 차려 (jeongsin charyeo) means "Get it together!", "Snap out of it!" or "Wake up!". People say it to someone who is distracted, foolish, in shock, or even fainting.
literal: 정신 means "mind" or "spirit", and 차려 is the casual command of 차리다, "to gather" or "to pull together". So literally it is "Pull your mind together."
usage: Say 정신 차려 to a friend who is daydreaming, making bad choices, or panicking. In K-dramas it is also shouted at someone who has collapsed, like "Stay with me!"
It is a casual command, so it can sound harsh. Use it with friends, family and younger people. People also say it to themselves: 정신 차리자 means "Come on, focus."
Use 정신 차리세요 for an older person who has fainted or is dazed. Telling an elder to get their act together is never polite, whatever the ending.

forms.en: Please wake up / Stay with me
forms.note: Polite, for someone dazed or fainting.

examples.context: Your friend is staring into space
Your friend wants to text their ex again
A classmate is dozing during a test

faq.q: What does jeongsin charyeo mean?
faq.a: 정신 차려 means "Get it together!" or "Snap out of it!". Literally it is "Pull your mind together."

faq.q: Is jeongsin charyeo rude?
faq.a: It is a casual command, so it can sound harsh. Use it with friends and younger people, not with elders.

faq.q: Why do K-drama characters say jeongsin charyeo to someone who fainted?
faq.a: Here it means "Wake up! Stay with me!", urging the person to regain consciousness.

intro: 와 (wa) means "Wow!" in Korean. People say it when they are impressed, amazed or shocked, and the tone tells you whether it is good or bad.
literal: 와 is a simple exclamation. Do not confuse it with the particle 와 ("and"), or with 와 meaning "come" in casual speech.
usage: Say 와 when you see something beautiful, taste something delicious, or hear surprising news. It often starts a longer reaction: 와 대박, 와 진짜, 와 예쁘다.
A long, flat 와... can mean you are speechless in a bad way, like "Wow... unbelievable." 우와 is a bigger, more excited "Wooow!"
와 is an exclamation, so it is fine around anyone, though what you say after it should match the person's level of politeness.

examples.context: Seeing a friend dressed up for a wedding
Tasting your grandmother's cooking
Looking out the window in winter

faq.q: What does wa mean in Korean?
faq.a: 와 means "Wow!". It shows amazement, and the tone can make it positive or disbelieving.

faq.q: What is the difference between wa and uwa?
faq.a: 우와 is a bigger, more excited version of 와, like "Wooow!"

faq.q: Is wa the same as the Korean word for and?
faq.a: No. The particle 와 ("and") is spelled the same but is a grammar word. The exclamation 와 is said on its own.

intro: 동생 (dongsaeng) means "younger sibling" and can refer to a younger brother or a younger sister. Koreans also use it for younger friends and acquaintances they feel close to, much like calling someone a little brother or little sister.
literal: 동생 is a Sino-Korean word, usually traced to characters meaning "same" and "born," as in born of the same parents.
usage: Anyone can say 동생, male or female. To be specific, add 남 (male) or 여 (female): 남동생 is a younger brother and 여동생 is a younger sister.

Koreans rarely call a younger sibling 동생 to their face. Older siblings usually just use the younger one's name, while the younger sibling calls them 오빠, 언니, 형 or 누나. 동생 is mostly used when talking about someone.
Outside the family, a phrase like 아는 동생 (a younger person I know) is a common way to describe a younger friend. Saying someone is "like a 동생 to me" shows warm, protective feelings.

forms.note: Makes clear you mean a blood relative.
Common way to describe a younger friend.

examples.context: Introducing your little sister to a friend
Asking a new classmate about their family
examples.en: Do you have a younger brother?

examples.context: Showing a friend a photo of your little brother
examples.en: My little brother is cute, right?

faq.q: Is dongsaeng a brother or a sister?
faq.a: It can be either. 동생 just means a younger sibling. Say 남동생 for a younger brother and 여동생 for a younger sister.

faq.q: Do Koreans call their younger sibling dongsaeng?
faq.a: Not usually when talking to them. Older siblings call younger ones by name, and use 동생 when talking about them to other people.

faq.q: Can a friend be my dongsaeng?
faq.a: Yes. Koreans often call a close younger friend a 동생, or describe them as 아는 동생, "a younger person I know."

intro: 엄마 (eomma) means "mom" or "mommy" and is the everyday word Koreans use for their mother. It is the first word many Korean babies learn, and plenty of adults keep calling their mother 엄마 their whole life.
literal: 엄마 is a native Korean word. The fuller, more respectful word for mother is 어머니.
usage: 엄마 is warm and casual. Children, teens and many grown adults use it at home, especially daughters. In formal situations, such as talking to a boss or writing a speech, adults switch to 어머니.
Koreans often say 우리 엄마, literally "our mom," even when they mean "my mom." This is completely normal and does not mean the mother is shared with the listener.
Do not call someone else's mother 엄마. For a friend's mother, say 어머님 or 어머니. 엄마야! on its own is also a common startled cry, like "Oh my gosh!"

forms.note: More respectful, used by adults and in formal speech.
Startled exclamation, not a way to call your mom.
Casual, typed shortening of 우리 엄마.

examples.context: A child coming home from school
Texting home while studying abroad
Bragging about your mother's cooking
examples.en: My mom is a great cook.

faq.q: What is the difference between eomma and eomeoni?
faq.a: Both mean mother. 엄마 is warm and casual, like "mom," while 어머니 is more respectful, like "mother," and is used in formal speech.

faq.q: Do Korean adults still say eomma?
faq.a: Yes, very often. Many adults call their mother 엄마 at home, though they may say 어머니 in formal settings.

faq.q: Why do Koreans say "our mom"?
faq.a: Korean often uses 우리 (our) for things closely tied to you, like your family or home. 우리 엄마 simply means "my mom."

intro: 아빠 (appa) means "dad" or "daddy" and is the everyday word Koreans use for their father. It is warm and casual, like "Dad" in English.
literal: 아빠 is a native Korean word. The fuller, more respectful word for father is 아버지.
usage: Children use 아빠 all the time, and many adults keep using it, especially daughters. Some sons start saying 아버지 as they grow up, particularly in more traditional families.
Like 엄마, it is often paired with 우리: 우리 아빠 means "my dad." You may also hear a wife call her husband 아빠 in front of the kids, as in "Ask Dad."
Do not use 아빠 for someone else's father. Say 아버님 or 아버지 instead, which sound respectful.

forms.note: More respectful, used in formal speech.
For someone else's father or a father-in-law.

forms.en: dad who dotes on his daughter

examples.context: Calling your dad on his birthday
A child waiting for dad to get home
Talking about your family in class
examples.en: My dad is a police officer.

faq.q: Is appa the same as abeoji?
faq.a: Both mean father. 아빠 is casual and warm, like "dad," while 아버지 is more respectful, like "father."

faq.q: Can grown-ups say appa?
faq.a: Yes. Plenty of adults, especially daughters, call their father 아빠 their whole life.

intro: 어머니 (eomeoni) means "mother." It is the respectful, standard word, while 엄마 is the casual, childlike "mom."
literal: 어머니 is a native Korean word. 엄마 is its softer everyday version.
usage: Adults use 어머니 when they want to sound respectful or formal, for example when talking about their mother to a teacher, a boss or someone older. Some people, often adult sons, also call their own mother 어머니 at home.
When speaking about your mother politely, Koreans use honorific verbs for her, such as 어머니께서 오셨어요 (my mother came), instead of the plain verbs.
For someone else's mother or a mother-in-law, 어머님 sounds even more respectful and is the more common choice.

forms.note: For someone else's mother or a mother-in-law.
Uses the honorific subject marker 께서.

examples.context: Calling your mother after a long time
Telling a teacher about your family
Explaining who made the side dishes

faq.q: What is the difference between eomeoni and eomma?
faq.a: They both mean mother. 엄마 is casual like "mom," and 어머니 is respectful like "mother."

faq.q: What is the difference between eomeoni and eomeonim?
faq.a: 어머님 adds the honorific 님 and is used mostly for other people's mothers and for a mother-in-law. 어머니 is the usual respectful word for your own mother.

intro: 아버지 (abeoji) means "father." It is the respectful, standard word, while 아빠 is the casual "dad."
literal: 아버지 is a native Korean word. 아빠 is its softer everyday version.
usage: Adults use 아버지 to talk about their father respectfully, for example to a teacher, coworker or someone older. Some people, especially sons in traditional families, also call their own father 아버지 directly.
Use honorific forms when talking about your father politely: 아버지께서 (as the subject) and 아버지께 (to Father).
For someone else's father or a father-in-law, say 아버님, which is even more respectful.

forms.note: For someone else's father or a father-in-law.

examples.context: Coming home and greeting your father
Introducing your family at a job interview
examples.en: My father is an office worker.

examples.context: Telling a sibling you checked in on Dad

faq.q: Is abeoji the same as appa?
faq.a: Both mean father. 아빠 is casual like "dad," while 아버지 is respectful like "father."

faq.q: Who do you call abeonim?
faq.a: 아버님 is for someone else's father or your father-in-law. It is more respectful than 아버지.

intro: 할머니 (halmeoni) means "grandmother" or "grandma." Koreans also use it as a respectful way to address or talk about any elderly woman.
literal: 할머니 is a native Korean word. It is often explained as coming from an old form meaning "big mother."
usage: Grandchildren call their grandmother 할머니, and many speak to her in casual speech because the relationship is close. Others use polite speech, depending on the family.
With strangers, 할머니 is a normal and respectful way to address a clearly elderly woman, for example when offering her your seat on the bus.
Be careful with women who are middle-aged rather than elderly. Calling a woman in her fifties 할머니 can offend her. 어머님 is a safer choice.

examples.context: Eating grandma's cooking
Telling a friend your weekend plans
Offering your seat to an elderly woman on the bus

faq.q: Is it rude to call an old woman halmeoni?
faq.a: No, it is normal and respectful for a clearly elderly woman. Just avoid it for women who are only middle-aged.

faq.q: What is the difference between oe-halmeoni and chin-halmeoni?
faq.a: 외할머니 is your mother's mother and 친할머니 is your father's mother. In everyday talk most people just say 할머니.

intro: 할아버지 (harabeoji) means "grandfather" or "grandpa." Koreans also use it as a respectful way to address or talk about any elderly man.
literal: 할아버지 is a native Korean word built around 아버지 (father).
usage: Grandchildren call their grandfather 할아버지. Families differ on whether kids use polite or casual speech with him, but honorific words like 진지 (meal) and 드세요 (please eat) are common when speaking to grandparents.
With strangers, 할아버지 is a normal, respectful way to address a clearly elderly man.
Avoid it for men who are only middle-aged, since it can make them feel old. 아버님 or a polite "excuse me" (저기요) works better.

examples.context: Calling grandpa to the table
Telling a friend where your grandfather lives
examples.en: My grandpa lives in the countryside.

examples.context: Saying goodbye after a holiday visit

faq.q: Can I call any old man harabeoji?
faq.a: Yes, for a clearly elderly man it is normal and polite. For a middle-aged man it can sound like you think he looks old.

faq.q: How do you spell harabeoji?
faq.a: The official romanization is harabeoji, but you will also see halabeoji and haraboji. They all mean 할아버지.

intro: 삼촌 (samchon) means "uncle," traditionally your father's younger, unmarried brother. Today Koreans also use it loosely for other uncles and as a friendly name for a man close to the family.
literal: 삼촌 is Sino-Korean and means "three 촌." A 촌 is a step of family distance, and an uncle is three steps away from you. A cousin is 사촌, four steps away.
usage: Strictly, 삼촌 is your father's brother who is not yet married. Once he marries, many families switch to 작은아버지 (younger uncle) or 큰아버지 (older uncle). Your mother's brother is 외삼촌.
Kids often call their parents' close male friends 삼촌, a bit like "Uncle Mike" in English. Some adults also call a younger male shop or restaurant worker 삼촌 to sound friendly.
An uncle often calls himself 삼촌 when talking to a nephew or niece, as in "Come play with Uncle!"

examples.context: A child asking an uncle for money on a holiday
examples.en: Uncle, give me some pocket money!

examples.context: Telling your mom that her brother arrived
An uncle inviting his little nephew to play

faq.q: Is samchon on the mom's side or dad's side?
faq.a: 삼촌 is traditionally your father's brother. Your mother's brother is 외삼촌, though in casual talk people often just say 삼촌.

faq.q: Why do Korean kids call family friends samchon?
faq.a: It is a warm way to treat a close family friend like a relative, much like calling someone "Uncle" in English even when he is not related.

intro: 이모 (imo) means "aunt," specifically your mother's sister. Koreans also use 이모 as a friendly way to call a middle-aged woman working at a restaurant or market.
literal: 이모 is a Sino-Korean family word for a mother's sister. Your father's sister has a different title, 고모.
usage: In the family, 이모 is only for your mother's sisters. Kids also call their mother's close female friends 이모, which feels warm and familiar.
At casual restaurants, customers often call the server or owner, usually a middle-aged woman, 이모. It sounds friendly and homey. 이모님 is a more polite version, also used for nannies and housekeepers.
Do not call a young woman 이모 in a restaurant. For younger staff, 저기요 (excuse me) is safer.

forms.note: Polite form for restaurant staff, nannies and caregivers.

examples.context: Asking for water at a casual restaurant
examples.en: Excuse me, could we get some water here?

examples.context: Telling a friend about a birthday gift
examples.en: My aunt bought me a present.

examples.context: Calling your aunt on the phone

faq.q: Why do Koreans call restaurant ladies imo?
faq.a: Calling the server 이모 makes the restaurant feel like a family kitchen. It is friendly and common at casual places, especially with middle-aged women.

faq.q: What is the difference between imo and gomo?
faq.a: 이모 is your mother's sister and 고모 is your father's sister.

intro: 아가씨 (agassi) means "young lady" or "miss" and refers to a young, unmarried woman. In historical dramas it also means "my lady," the daughter of a noble family.
literal: In older Korean, 아가씨 was a respectful word for a young lady from a well-off or noble household, which is why servants use it in historical dramas.
usage: Older people sometimes use 아가씨 to address a young woman they do not know, like "Miss." Many young women today find it old-fashioned or a little condescending from strangers, so it is best not to use it yourself.
In the family, a married woman calls her husband's younger sister 아가씨. This is a standard in-law title, and it is respectful, not rude.
In historical dramas, servants call the daughter of the house 아가씨, much like "my lady" or "young mistress."

forms.note: Male counterpart in historical dramas and in-law titles.

examples.context: An older man telling a young woman she dropped something
A woman offering tea to her husband's younger sister
A servant speaking to a noble daughter in a historical drama
examples.en: My lady, where are you going?

faq.q: Is agassi rude?
faq.a: It is not a rude word, but from a stranger it can sound old-fashioned or talking down to a young woman. Learners should avoid using it to address strangers.

faq.q: Why does a wife call her sister-in-law agassi?
faq.a: It is the traditional title a married woman uses for her husband's younger sister. It sounds polite within the family.

intro: 선생님 (seonsaengnim) means "teacher" and is the respectful way to address one. Koreans also use it as a polite title for doctors and other respected professionals.
literal: 선생 is Sino-Korean, from characters meaning "born first," and 님 is an honorific suffix.
usage: Students call their teachers 선생님, either alone or after the surname, like 김 선생님. Koreans do not usually call teachers by their first name.
It is also how you address doctors, nurses, counselors, lawyers and artists. When you are unsure what to call a professional adult, 선생님 is often a safe, respectful choice.
Students casually shorten it to 쌤. That is fine among students, but do not say 쌤 to a teacher you are not close with.

forms.note: Without 님 it can sound like you are talking down, so use it only when not addressing someone.

examples.context: Raising your hand in class
Thanking a doctor after an appointment
Calling the school office

faq.q: Can I call my Korean tutor seonsaengnim?
faq.a: Yes, that is exactly right and shows respect, even if your tutor is young.

faq.q: Why do Koreans call doctors seonsaengnim?
faq.a: 선생님 is a general title of respect for professionals, so patients use it for doctors, much like saying "Doctor" in English.

faq.q: What does ssaem mean?
faq.a: 쌤 is a casual student shortening of 선생님, used among students and with teachers they are close to.

intro: 사장님 (sajangnim) means "boss" or "company president," with an honorific attached. Koreans also use it to politely address the owner of a shop, restaurant or small business.
literal: 사장 is Sino-Korean for the head of a company, and 님 is an honorific suffix.
usage: Employees call the head of their company 사장님. In a bigger company you will also hear other titles, like 부장님 (department head) or 대표님 (CEO).
In daily life, 사장님 is the polite, friendly way to call the owner at a restaurant, cafe or market stall. People use it even when they are not sure the person is the actual owner.
Avoid saying just 사장 without 님 when you speak to the person. On its own it is used to talk about the role, not to address someone.

forms.note: Used to talk about the role.
Common title at startups and small firms.
Head of a large business group.

examples.context: Asking for the bill at a restaurant
A coworker passing on a message
examples.en: The boss is calling for you.

examples.context: Saying goodbye to a market vendor

faq.q: Can I call a restaurant owner sajangnim?
faq.a: Yes. It is one of the most common and polite ways to get the owner's or staff's attention at a restaurant.

faq.q: Is sajangnim only for the CEO?
faq.a: No. It can mean a company president, but in everyday life it is also a polite title for any business owner.

intro: 남친 (namchin) means "boyfriend." It is a casual short form of 남자 친구, which literally means "male friend."
literal: 남친 takes the first syllable of 남자 (man) and the first syllable of 친구 (friend).
usage: 남친 is used constantly in speech and texts by people of all ages. In more careful or formal situations, people say the full 남자 친구.
Even though the full form literally means "male friend," 남자 친구 almost always means a romantic boyfriend. A guy who is just a friend is a 남사친.
전 남친 or 전남친 means an ex-boyfriend.

forms.note: Full form, fine in any situation.
Platonic male friend, short for 남자 사람 친구.

examples.context: Sharing big news with a friend
Telling a friend about your weekend
examples.en: I watched a movie with my boyfriend.

examples.context: A coworker asking a personal question

faq.q: Is namchin slang?
faq.a: It is a casual shortening, but it is so common that everyone uses it. In formal writing, use 남자 친구.

faq.q: Does namja chingu just mean a male friend?
faq.a: Usually not. 남자 친구 normally means boyfriend. For a male friend with no romance, Koreans say 남사친 or simply 친구.

intro: 여친 (yeochin) means "girlfriend." It is a casual short form of 여자 친구, which literally means "female friend."
literal: 여친 takes the first syllable of 여자 (woman) and the first syllable of 친구 (friend).
usage: 여친 is everywhere in casual speech and texting. In more careful situations, say the full 여자 친구.
Just like 남자 친구, 여자 친구 almost always means a romantic partner. A female friend with no romance is a 여사친.
전 여친 or 전여친 means an ex-girlfriend.

forms.note: Full form, fine in any situation.
Platonic female friend, short for 여자 사람 친구.

examples.context: Complaining to a friend after a breakup
examples.en: I got dumped by my girlfriend.

examples.context: Thinking about an anniversary gift
examples.en: What should I get my girlfriend?

examples.context: Introducing your girlfriend to a senior

faq.q: Is yeochin slang?
faq.a: It is a casual shortening that everyone uses. In formal situations, say 여자 친구.

faq.q: How do you say "girl friend" without meaning girlfriend?
faq.a: Say 여사친 or just 친구. 여자 친구 usually means a romantic girlfriend.

intro: 애인 (aein) means "sweetheart," "lover" or "partner," the person you are dating. It works for a boyfriend or a girlfriend.
literal: 애인 is Sino-Korean, made of characters meaning "love" and "person."
usage: 애인 is gender neutral, so it is handy when you do not want to say boyfriend or girlfriend. 애인 있어요? is a common way to ask if someone is seeing anyone.
Younger people tend to say 남친 or 여친 in casual talk, so 애인 can sound a little more grown-up. It does not mean an affair partner in Korean, even though the same characters can mean that in Japanese.
For a couple seen from outside, as in "they are lovers," Koreans often use 연인 instead, which sounds more literary.

examples.context: A friend asking about your love life
Telling a close friend some sad news
examples.en: I broke up with my partner.

examples.context: Promising a friend something
examples.en: When I get a partner, I'll introduce you.

faq.q: Does aein mean a secret lover?
faq.a: No. In Korean 애인 simply means the person you are dating. It does not suggest an affair.

faq.q: Is aein for boys or girls?
faq.a: Both. 애인 works for any partner, which makes it a neutral word.

intro: 공주 (gongju) means "princess." You hear it for real royalty in historical dramas, and parents and partners also use it as a sweet nickname, as in 우리 공주, "my princess."
literal: 공주 is a Sino-Korean word for a king's daughter.
usage: In historical dramas, characters address a princess as 공주님 or 공주 마마, with extra honorifics.
Parents often call a young daughter 우리 공주 (our princess), and boyfriends sometimes call their girlfriend 공주님 in a sweet, playful way.
공주병, literally "princess disease," is a teasing word for a girl who acts like she is a princess or thinks she is extremely pretty.

forms.note: Common pet name for a daughter.

examples.context: A dad waking up his little daughter
A court lady guiding a princess in a historical drama
Teasing a friend who takes too many selfies
examples.en: Do you think you're a princess?

faq.q: Is calling someone gongju a compliment?
faq.a: Usually it is sweet, especially from a parent or partner. 공주병, though, is teasing and means someone acts spoiled.

faq.q: What does gongjunim mean?
faq.a: 공주님 is 공주 plus the honorific 님. It is how people respectfully address a princess, or a sweet way to call a girlfriend or daughter.

intro: 님 (nim) is an honorific suffix that shows respect. Koreans attach it to titles and names, as in 선생님 (teacher), 사장님 (boss) and 고객님 (customer).
literal: 님 is a native Korean word that has long expressed respect. In old poems and songs, 님 alone can also mean a dear, beloved person.
usage: Most often 님 is stuck onto a job title or role: 선생님, 사장님, 의사 선생님, 부모님 (parents). It turns a plain title into a respectful way of addressing someone.
Online and at work, people put 님 after a name or username to be polite to someone they do not know well, like 민지 님. It is more respectful than 씨.
Never put 님 after your own name or title. You use it only for other people.

forms.note: Used by fans for authors and webtoon artists.
Casual online way to address readers.

examples.context: Replying to a coworker's message
A store clerk asking a customer to wait
Meeting a favorite webtoon artist
examples.en: I'm a big fan of yours.

faq.q: What does nim mean after a name?
faq.a: It adds respect, a bit like a very polite "Mr." or "Ms." Koreans use it for people they do not know well, especially at work or online.

faq.q: What is the difference between nim and ssi?
faq.a: Both are polite, but 님 is more respectful. 씨 goes after names of equals or juniors, while 님 can be used for anyone you want to honor.

faq.q: Can I add nim to my own name?
faq.a: No. Using 님 for yourself sounds like you are praising yourself.

intro: 씨 (ssi) is a polite title that goes after someone's name, like "Mr." or "Ms." For example, 지은 씨 is a polite way to address a woman named Jieun.
usage: Put 씨 after a full name (김지은 씨) or a given name (지은 씨). This is common between coworkers and adults of similar age who are not close friends.
Do not put 씨 after a surname alone, like 김 씨. That sounds cold or even talking down. Also avoid 씨 for someone clearly older or higher in rank. Use their title, such as 선생님 or 부장님.
Never use 씨 for yourself. When Koreans introduce themselves, they just say their name.

forms.note: Full name plus 씨, a bit more formal.

examples.context: Offering coffee to a coworker
examples.en: Jieun, would you like some coffee?

examples.context: Getting to know a new classmate
Thanking a coworker who helped you

faq.q: Can I call my boss ssi?
faq.a: No. For a boss or anyone senior, use their title, like 팀장님 or 사장님. 씨 is for equals or juniors.

faq.q: Is it rude to say Kim ssi?
faq.a: Surname plus 씨, like 김 씨, can sound rude or distant. Use the given name or full name with 씨 instead.

intro: 오라버니 (orabeoni) means "older brother" and is the old-fashioned, respectful form of 오빠. Like 오빠, it is used only by girls and women, and today you mostly hear it in historical dramas.
literal: 오라버니 is the older, more formal version of 오빠. Both are native Korean words.
usage: In historical dramas, sisters and young noblewomen call their older brothers 오라버니, usually with formal speech.
In modern life, almost no one uses 오라버니 seriously. A woman might use it as a joke to sound extra polite or dramatic, for example when she wants a favor from an older male friend.
Just like 오빠, it is only said by females. Males use 형 or 형님.

examples.context: A noblewoman in a historical drama seeing her brother off
A sister greeting her brother after a long trip
A maid announcing a visitor to the young lady

faq.q: Is orabeoni the same as oppa?
faq.a: Yes, it means the same thing. 오라버니 is the old-fashioned, formal form, and 오빠 is what people say today.

faq.q: Can I call my idol orabeoni?
faq.a: You can as a joke. It will sound playful and dramatic, like something from a historical drama.

intro: 형님 (hyungnim) is the respectful form of 형 (hyung), so it means a respected "older brother." Men use it for older men they look up to, and it is also an important in-law title in Korean families.
literal: 형님 is 형 (older brother) plus the honorific suffix 님.
usage: A man calls an older man 형님 when he wants to show extra respect, for example a much older friend, a senior at work, or a brother-in-law. In movies, gang members famously call their boss 형님.
In families, a woman calls her husband's older brother's wife 형님, and often her husband's older sister too. A man calls his wife's older brother or his wife's older sister's husband 형님.
With a close older friend, plain 형 is enough. Using 형님 there can sound stiff or jokingly formal.

forms.note: Used in families and in gangster movies.

examples.context: Two men meeting again after years
Pouring a drink for an older man at dinner
A woman helping her sister-in-law cook during the holidays

faq.q: Can a woman say hyungnim?
faq.a: Yes, in one special case: married women call certain female in-laws, like the husband's older brother's wife, 형님. Otherwise women say 오빠 or 오라버니.

faq.q: Why do gangsters say hyungnim?
faq.a: In crime movies and dramas, 형님 shows loyalty and respect to the boss, so the word is strongly linked with that image.

faq.q: Is hyungnim more polite than hyung?
faq.a: Yes. 님 adds respect, so 형님 is more formal and respectful than 형.

intro: 어머님 (eomeonim) is a very respectful word for "mother." Koreans use it for a mother-in-law, a friend's or partner's mother, and as a polite way to address middle-aged women.
literal: 어머님 is 어머니 (mother) plus the honorific suffix 님.
usage: A married woman calls her husband's mother 어머님. Many husbands also call their wife's mother 어머님 to her face, even though the title for her is 장모님.
When you meet a friend's or partner's mother, 어머님 is the polite way to greet her. You also hear salespeople and service staff use it to address middle-aged women customers.
For your own mother, people usually say 엄마 or 어머니, not 어머님.

forms.note: Respectful word, used for your own mother.

examples.context: Meeting your partner's mother for the first time
A clothing store clerk helping a customer
Complimenting a friend's mom at dinner

faq.q: What is the difference between eomeoni and eomeonim?
faq.a: 어머님 has the honorific 님, so it is more respectful. It is used for other people's mothers and in-laws, while 어머니 is used for your own mother.

faq.q: Why do shop staff call women eomeonim?
faq.a: It is a polite, warm way to address a middle-aged customer. Many find it nicer than 아줌마, which can sound blunt.

intro: 우리 (uri) means "we" or "our." Koreans also use it where English uses "my," as in 우리 엄마 (my mom) or 우리 집 (my home).
usage: As "we," 우리 works like in English: 우리 가자 means "Let's go (us)." Starting a suggestion with 우리 makes it feel friendly and inclusive.

As "our," it shows closeness and belonging. Koreans say 우리 엄마, 우리 회사 (my company) and even 우리 남편 (my husband) without meaning the listener shares them. Fans also say 우리 오빠 or 우리 애들 for their favorite idols.
In polite or formal speech, when the listener is not part of the group, the humble form 저희 is used instead, as in 저희 회사. Do not use 저희 for Korea itself, though: it is always 우리나라.

forms.note: Polite form when talking to someone outside the group.
How Koreans refer to their own country.

examples.context: Inviting a friend over
Making a new friend at school
A fan cheering for a favorite idol

faq.q: Why do Koreans say "our" instead of "my"?
faq.a: Korean culture puts weight on the group, so 우리 is used for family, home, school and country. 우리 엄마 just means "my mom."

faq.q: What is the difference between uri and jeohui?
faq.a: Both mean we or our. 저희 is the humble, polite form used when speaking to someone outside your group, and 우리 is the everyday form.

faq.q: Do married women really say "our husband"?
faq.a: Yes. 우리 남편 is completely normal and simply means "my husband." No one takes it literally.

intro: 나도 (nado) means "me too" in Korean. It is casual, so you say it to friends, partners and younger people. It is also the start of many replies, like 나도 사랑해, "I love you too."
literal: 나 (na) is the casual word for "I" or "me," and 도 (do) is a particle that means "also" or "too." Put together, 나도 is simply "me too."
usage: You can use 나도 on its own as a full reply, or put it in front of a sentence: 나도 배고파 means "I'm hungry too." The same 도 also works with negatives, so 나도 몰라 means "I don't know either."
With teachers, bosses or anyone older you are not close to, switch to the humble 저도 (jeodo), and add 요 when it stands alone: 저도요, "Me too."
A common beginner mistake is answering an older person with 나도. It is not rude among friends, but to an elder it sounds too casual.

forms.note: Humble and polite; safe with anyone.
Casual; literally "I am like that too."
도 works with negative sentences too.

examples.context: A friend says they are starving
Replying to a partner's "I love you"
A friend says the exam was too hard

faq.q: What is the difference between nado and jeodo?
faq.a: Both mean "me too." 나도 uses the casual word for "I," and 저도 uses the humble word for "I," so 저도 (or 저도요) is the one to use with older people and strangers.

faq.q: How do you say "me neither" in Korean?
faq.a: Also with 나도. Korean uses the same 도 for "too" and "either," so 나도 안 갈래 means "I'm not going either."

intro: 뽀뽀 (ppoppo) means a kiss in Korean, usually a quick, light peck. It is a cute, gentle word that parents use with small children and couples use with each other. A deeper, romantic kiss is usually called 키스 (kiseu).
literal: 뽀뽀 is a native Korean word with a soft, babyish sound, a bit like "smooch" in English. To say "to kiss," add 하다: 뽀뽀하다.
usage: Parents ask their kids for a 뽀뽀 all the time, and grandparents tease little ones with it. Between couples it sounds sweet and playful rather than serious.
If someone in a drama asks for a 뽀뽀 while pointing at their cheek, they mean a peck on the cheek, which is called 볼뽀뽀 or 볼에 뽀뽀.
Because it is a cute word, it fits casual, affectionate moments. In news or formal writing you will see 입맞춤 or 키스 instead.

forms.note: From English; a longer, romantic kiss.

examples.context: A mom asking her toddler for a kiss
Being playful with a partner
Telling a friend about a date
examples.en: He kissed me on the cheek.

faq.q: What is the difference between ppoppo and kiseu?
faq.a: 뽀뽀 is a light, quick kiss and sounds cute, the kind you give a child or a quick peck to a partner. 키스 (kiseu) means a longer, romantic kiss.

faq.q: Is ppoppo only for kids?
faq.a: No. Adults say it too, especially couples being sweet with each other. It just has a soft, cute feel.

intro: 고백 (gobaek) means "confession" in Korean, and in dating it means telling someone you like them, usually while asking them to be your boyfriend or girlfriend. It is a big moment in Korean dating culture and in almost every K-drama romance.
literal: It is a Sino-Korean word made of 告 (to tell) and 白 (to state or make clear). To say "to confess," add 하다: 고백하다.
usage: In Korea, a relationship often officially starts with a 고백. Someone says they like the other person and asks to date, and if the answer is yes, many couples count their anniversaries from that day.
You 고백하다 (confess) and the other person 고백을 받다 (receives a confession). Getting turned down after confessing is often described as 차였어, "I got dumped."
Outside of romance, 고백 still means a confession in general, like admitting a secret or a mistake.

forms.note: Dictionary form; usually means confessing feelings.

examples.context: Telling a friend big news
Building up courage before a date
Telling a coworker about a surprise

faq.q: What does confess mean in K-dramas?
faq.a: It means telling someone you have feelings for them and, usually, asking them out. A 고백 is what turns a crush or a 썸 into an official relationship.

faq.q: Is gobaek only about love?
faq.a: No. It can mean any confession, such as admitting a secret or something you did. In everyday talk about dating, though, it almost always means confessing feelings.

intro: 소개팅 (sogaeting) means a blind date in Korean, usually a one-on-one meeting set up by a friend. It is one of the most common ways young Koreans meet someone to date.
literal: It is 소개 (sogae), "introduction," plus 팅, taken from the English word "meeting." So it is literally an "introduction meeting."
usage: A friend or coworker who knows both people arranges it, shares phone numbers, and the two meet for coffee or a meal. Asking a friend 소개팅 시켜 줘 ("set me up") is very common and not embarrassing.
A 미팅 (miting) is the group version, popular with college students. A 맞선 or 선 is a more serious arranged meeting, often set up by family with marriage in mind.
After a 소개팅, friends will always ask how it went and whether there was 애프터, a second date.

forms.en: To go on a blind date
Set me up on a blind date

forms.note: Several people from each side meet together.
Formal matchmaking, usually with marriage in mind.

examples.context: Asking a friend for help
examples.en: Set me up on a blind date.

examples.context: Explaining why you can't hang out
examples.en: I have a blind date tomorrow.

examples.context: Asking a coworker the next day

faq.q: What is the difference between sogaeting and miting?
faq.a: 소개팅 is one-on-one, set up by a friend. 미팅 is a group blind date where several people from each side meet at once.

faq.q: Is a sogaeting serious?
faq.a: Not very. It is a casual first meeting to see if you click. A 맞선 (matseon) is the more serious, marriage-minded version.

intro: 스킨십 (skinship) means physical affection or touch in Korean, like holding hands, hugging or kissing. It is a Konglish word you will hear a lot when people talk about dating, and also about parents and children.
literal: It was made in Korean from the English words "skin" and "-ship," like "friendship." English speakers do not use it this way, so it often confuses learners.
usage: For couples, 스킨십 covers everything from holding hands to kissing. People talk about how fast a couple's 스킨십 is moving, or whether someone is the type who likes a lot of it.
It is not only romantic. Parents are encouraged to give babies lots of 스킨십, and close friends may be described as having a lot of 스킨십 if they hug and link arms.
It is a neutral, everyday word, not crude. You can use it with friends or in polite conversation.

forms.note: Describes a person or a couple.

forms.en: How far a couple has gone physically

forms.note: Often the first step of 스킨십 for a new couple.

examples.context: Asking a new partner gently
Talking about a new relationship
examples.en: Things are getting physical too fast.

examples.context: Describing your dating style

faq.q: Is skinship an English word?
faq.a: No. It is Konglish, a word made in Korea from English parts. Native English speakers would say "physical affection" or "PDA."

faq.q: Does skinship mean something sexual?
faq.a: Not by itself. It covers any affectionate touch, including hugs, holding hands and a parent cuddling a child.

intro: 정 (jeong) means a deep, warm attachment that grows between people over time in Korean. It is the bond you feel for family, old friends, neighbors, and even people you argue with, and many Koreans see it as a core part of their culture.
literal: It is a Sino-Korean word from 情, which means feeling or affection. Orion's Choco Pie famously prints 情 on its box to sell the snack as a way of sharing warmth.
usage: 정 is not quite love and not quite friendship. It builds slowly from time spent together, shared meals and small kindnesses, which is why people say 정이 들었어, "I've grown attached."
Someone who is 정이 많다 is warm-hearted and generous, like a grandmother who always sends you home with food. When 정이 떨어지다 ("affection falls off"), it means you have been turned off by someone.
Koreans also talk about 미운 정 고운 정, the attachment that comes from both the annoying and the lovely moments, often said about long marriages and family.

forms.en: To be turned off, lose affection
forms.note: Said when someone's behavior ruins your feelings.

forms.en: Attachment through good times and bad

examples.context: Moving away from a neighborhood
Talking about your grandma
Complaining about a rude date

faq.q: Is there an English word for jeong?
faq.a: Not exactly. "Affection," "attachment" and "fondness" each cover part of it. 정 is the bond that grows with time and shared life, even with people you do not always like.

faq.q: What does jeong-i deureosseo mean?
faq.a: 정이 들었어 means "I've grown attached." People say it about a place, a pet, coworkers or a person they have spent a lot of time with.

intro: 내 꺼 (nae kkeo) means "mine" in Korean. It is the way people actually say it out loud, and it shows up in flirting as 너는 내 꺼야, "you're mine." The standard spelling is 내 거, but 내 꺼 is very common in texts and song titles.
literal: 내 (nae) means "my," and 거 (geo) is a spoken short form of 것, "thing." Because 거 is pronounced with a hard sound after 내, many people write it 꺼.
usage: In everyday life it just means "mine," like claiming the last piece of chicken: 이거 내 꺼야.
In romance it is a sweet, slightly possessive line. 내 꺼 하자 ("be mine") is a classic, cheesy way to ask someone out.
In school or formal writing, use the standard spelling 내 거 or 내 것. Spelling it 꺼 is fine in casual texts but counts as a spelling mistake on a test.

forms.note: Cheesy, cute way to ask someone out.

examples.context: Grabbing the last snack
A playful text to a partner
Asking a crush out

faq.q: Is it nae kkeo or nae geo?
faq.a: The standard spelling is 내 거 (nae geo), but it is pronounced closer to 내 꺼, so that spelling is everywhere in texts, songs and social media.

faq.q: Is nae kkeo romantic?
faq.a: It can be. On its own it just means "mine," but said about a person, like 너는 내 꺼야, it is a sweet, flirty way to say "you're mine."

intro: 예뻐 (yeppeo) means "you're pretty" or "it's pretty" in Korean. It is the casual form of 예쁘다, used with friends, partners and kids. You can say it about people, clothes, places and things.
literal: It comes from the adjective 예쁘다 (yeppeuda), "to be pretty." In Korean, adjectives work like verbs, so 예뻐 alone is a full sentence: "(You are) pretty."
usage: Korean drops the subject when it is clear, so the same 예뻐 can mean "you're pretty," "she's pretty" or "that's pretty" depending on the situation.
Older people often use 예쁘다 for children and pets to mean "sweet" or "lovely," including their behavior. 예쁜 짓 is a cute thing a child does.
You will also hear 이뻐 (ippeo). It is a common spoken version and is now accepted in the dictionary too. Add 요 to be polite: 예뻐요.

forms.note: Dictionary form; also said as an exclamation.

examples.context: Complimenting a partner
Shopping with a friend
Seeing cherry blossoms

faq.q: Is yeppeo only for girls?
faq.a: It is mostly said about women, kids, pets and things. For men, people usually say 잘생겼어 (handsome) or 멋있어 (cool), though a pretty-looking man can be called 예쁘다 too.

faq.q: What is the difference between yeppeo and ippeo?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. 예뻐 is the traditional standard spelling, and 이뻐 is a common spoken form that is now also accepted as standard.

intro: 귀여워 (gwiyeowo) means "you're cute" or "so cute" in Korean. It is the casual form of 귀엽다, and people say it about babies, pets, partners, idols and even small things like a tiny cup. Fans often type it as "kiyowo."
literal: It comes from the adjective 귀엽다 (gwiyeopda), "to be cute." The ㅂ at the end of the stem changes to 워 in this form, which is why 귀엽다 becomes 귀여워.
usage: It is one of the most used compliments in Korean. Couples say it to each other, and fans say it about idols doing 애교.
It is casual, so add 요 for politeness: 귀여워요. Calling your boss "cute" is risky, the same as in English, but grandparents and older friends will usually take it warmly.
A playful way to show how cute something is: 귀여워 죽겠어, "so cute I could die."

forms.note: Dictionary form; also said as an exclamation.
Slang nickname for a cute person.

examples.context: Seeing a friend's new puppy
Watching a baby laugh
examples.en: It's so cute I could die.

examples.context: Talking to a parent at the park

faq.q: What does kiyowo mean?
faq.a: It is a fan spelling of 귀여워 (gwiyeowo), "so cute." You will see it a lot in comments on idol videos.

faq.q: Can I call a guy gwiyeowo?
faq.a: Yes. It is a common, friendly compliment for men too, especially from a partner or fans.

intro: 멋있어 (meosisseo) means "you're cool," "that's cool" or "awesome" in Korean. It is the casual form of 멋있다, and it praises someone's style, attitude or actions. It is also a common way to say a man looks great.
literal: 멋 (meot) means style or flair, and 있다 (itda) means "to have." So 멋있다 is "to have style." It is pronounced roughly "muh-shi-ssuh."
usage: You can say it about a person, an outfit, a view, a performance or a brave decision. It works for women too: a confident woman can be very 멋있어.
Fans say it about idols on stage, and people often use it for a man where English might say "hot" or "handsome" in a respectful way.
It is casual. Use 멋있어요 with people you are polite with. A close word is 멋지다, which means almost the same thing.

examples.context: Watching a friend perform
Talking about a crush
On a mountain top

faq.q: What is the difference between meosisseo and jalsaenggyeosseo?
faq.a: 잘생겼어 is only about a handsome face. 멋있어 is about style, charm and attitude, so someone can be 멋있어 without being classically handsome.

faq.q: Can you say meosisseo to a woman?
faq.a: Yes. It praises confidence and style, so it is a great compliment for anyone.

intro: 잘생겼어 (jalsaenggyeosseo) means "you're handsome" or "he's good-looking" in Korean. It is the casual form of 잘생기다 and is mostly said about men. It is in the past tense, but it describes how someone looks now.
literal: 잘 means "well" and 생기다 means "to be formed" or "to come into being." So 잘생기다 is "to be well formed." Because it is a verb, Korean uses the past form 잘생겼어 to describe someone's looks, literally "(you) came out well."
usage: The past tense trips up many learners. 잘생겼어 does not mean someone used to be handsome. It means they are handsome. The same goes for its opposite, 못생겼어 (ugly).
It is mostly used for men. For women people usually say 예뻐, though 잘생겼다 is sometimes used for a woman with striking, handsome features.
Add 요 to be polite: 잘생겼어요. 잘생긴 goes before a noun: 잘생긴 남자, "a handsome man."

forms.note: Plain form; used as an exclamation.

examples.context: Complimenting a partner
Asking about a friend's new boyfriend
Seeing a photo of a friend's brother
examples.en: He's even more handsome than an actor!

faq.q: Why is jalsaenggyeosseo in the past tense?
faq.a: 잘생기다 is a verb meaning "to be formed well," so Korean describes the finished result with the past form. It means "is handsome," not "was handsome."

faq.q: Can jalsaenggyeosseo be used for women?
faq.a: Sometimes, for a woman with strong, handsome features. Most of the time people say 예뻐 (pretty) for women.

intro: 사귀자 (sagwija) means "let's go out" or "be my boyfriend/girlfriend" in Korean. It is the casual, direct way to ask someone to date you, often said right after a 고백 (confession).
literal: It comes from 사귀다 (sagwida), "to date" or "to get to know someone closely," plus -자 (-ja), which means "let's." So 사귀자 is literally "let's date."
usage: In Korea, dating usually becomes official with a clear question like 사귀자 or 나랑 사귈래? ("Will you go out with me?"). Many couples count their anniversaries from the day one of them said it.
It is casual, so it is for people your age or younger, or people you are already close to. A softer, polite version is 저랑 사귈래요?
사귀다 also means making friends, as in 친구를 사귀다, "to make a friend." Context tells you which one it is.

forms.en: Will you go out with me?

examples.context: Asking a crush out
Making it official after a date
After you both admit your feelings

faq.q: How do you ask someone out in Korean?
faq.a: The most common ways are 사귀자 ("let's go out") and 나랑 사귈래? ("will you go out with me?"). Use 저랑 사귈래요? to be polite.

faq.q: Does sagwida mean to date?
faq.a: Yes, in romance it means to date or be in a relationship. It can also mean to make friends, like 친구를 사귀다.

intro: 헤어지자 (heeojija) means "let's break up" in Korean. It is the casual, direct way to end a relationship, and one of the most dramatic lines in any K-drama.
literal: It comes from 헤어지다 (heeojida), "to part" or "to separate," plus -자 (-ja), "let's." So it is literally "let's part ways."
usage: Said between partners, it is serious. Saying it in a small fight and taking it back later is a common source of drama, so many people warn against using it lightly.
To say you already broke up, use the past tense: 우리 헤어졌어, "we broke up."
헤어지다 also simply means to say goodbye and part, like friends heading home after dinner. 헤어지기 싫어 can mean "I don't want to say goodbye (tonight)."

forms.en: Let's break up / We're breaking up (polite)

forms.note: Often said at the end of a date.

examples.context: Ending a relationship
Tired of fighting
A firm, final decision

faq.q: How do you say "we broke up" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 우리 헤어졌어 (uri heeojyeosseo). Politely, 헤어졌어요.

faq.q: Does heeojida only mean breaking up?
faq.a: No. It also means parting ways in general, like friends saying goodbye after hanging out.

intro: 당신 (dangsin) means "you" in Korean, but it is rarely used to talk to people face to face. Married couples use it like "honey" or "dear," songs, poems and ads use it as a gentle "you," and in an argument with a stranger it sounds hostile.
literal: It is a Sino-Korean word from 當身. Korean usually avoids "you" in conversation and uses names and titles instead, which is why 당신 has such specific uses.
usage: Between husband and wife, especially middle-aged and older couples, 당신 is a warm, everyday word, often alongside 여보.
With strangers it is risky. Lines like 당신이 뭔데? ("Who do you think you are?") show how it can sound cold or confrontational. To address someone politely, use their name with 씨, or a title like 선생님.
In lyrics, letters and advertisements, 당신 is a soft, respectful "you" aimed at the listener or reader.

forms.note: Sounds like a song lyric or a letter.

forms.en: Who do you think you are?

examples.context: A wife asking her husband
An anniversary card to a spouse
Snapping at a stranger in a fight (rude)

faq.q: Can I call someone dangsin?
faq.a: Usually not. With people you do not know, it can sound rude. Use their name with 씨 or a title instead. It is safe between spouses.

faq.q: Why do Korean songs say dangsin so much?
faq.a: In songs and poems 당신 is a soft, respectful "you" for a loved one, and it fits the gentle tone of a ballad.

intro: 내 사랑 (nae sarang) means "my love" in Korean. People use it as a sweet name for a partner, and parents and grandparents say it to children and even pets.
literal: 내 (nae) means "my," and 사랑 (sarang) means "love." Like in English, it can name the feeling or the person you love.
usage: It is affectionate and a little cheesy, the same as "my love" in English. It works well in texts, cards and sleepy good nights.
Parents often say 우리 딸 내 사랑 or 우리 아들 내 사랑 ("my daughter, my love") in birthday messages.
In songs and poems you may see 내 사랑아, with the calling ending 아, which sounds old-fashioned and dramatic.

forms.note: Poetic, dramatic way of calling someone.

examples.context: A good night text to a partner
Calling out to a partner leaving the room
examples.en: Where are you going, my love?

examples.context: A birthday message to a child

faq.q: Is nae sarang romantic only?
faq.a: No. It is used for partners, but parents and grandparents also call children 내 사랑.

faq.q: What is the difference between nae sarang and jagiya?
faq.a: 자기야 is the everyday "honey" couples call each other. 내 사랑 is sweeter and a bit more dramatic, so it shows up more in messages and special moments.

intro: 사랑 (sarang) means "love" in Korean. It is the noun, the way you would say "love" in "first love" or "love story." To say "I love you," you turn it into a verb: 사랑해.
literal: 사랑 is the everyday Korean noun for love. Its older history is debated, so the simple version is enough: add 하다 (to do) and it becomes the verb 사랑하다, "to love."
usage: You will find 사랑 in countless song titles, drama names and phrases like 첫사랑 (first love) and 짝사랑 (one-sided love).
It covers every kind of love: romantic, family, friends, and love for a country or a hobby.
A common phrase is 사랑에 빠지다, "to fall in love." Learners sometimes say 사랑 when they mean "I love you." The noun alone just means "love," so use 사랑해.

examples.context: Telling a friend the big news
Confused about new feelings
After a hard week in a relationship

faq.q: What is the difference between sarang and saranghae?
faq.a: 사랑 is the noun "love." 사랑해 is the verb form and means "I love you."

faq.q: How do you say "fall in love" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 사랑에 빠지다. "I fell in love" is 사랑에 빠졌어.

intro: 짝사랑 (jjaksarang) means one-sided or unrequited love in Korean. It is when you like someone who does not like you back, or who does not even know. It is one of the most popular themes in K-dramas and ballads.
literal: 짝 (jjak) is a word about pairs and one half of a pair, and 사랑 means love. So 짝사랑 is love from just one side.
usage: You can use it as a noun (나 짝사랑 중이야, "I have a one-sided crush") or a verb with 하다 (선배를 짝사랑해요, "I have a crush on my senior").
It often suggests a secret crush that has gone on for a while, sometimes with a little heartache.
When the feelings turn out to be mutual, people may say it was 쌍방, "both sides," and the 짝사랑 becomes a 썸 or a relationship.

forms.note: Literally "in the middle of one-sided love."

examples.context: Telling a close friend a secret
Confessing to a diary or friend
examples.en: I have a crush on my senior.

examples.context: Complaining late at night

faq.q: Is jjaksarang the same as a crush?
faq.a: Close. A 짝사랑 is a crush that is not returned, or not yet. If the other person likes you too, it is no longer 짝사랑.

faq.q: How do you say "I have a crush on you" in Korean?
faq.a: Most people would say 좋아해 ("I like you") directly. 짝사랑 is more for talking about the crush to someone else.

intro: 첫사랑 (cheotsarang) means "first love" in Korean. It can mean the feeling or the person, and it is one of the most loved themes in Korean dramas, films and songs.
literal: 첫 (cheot) means "first," and 사랑 (sarang) means "love." Together they make one word, written without a space.
usage: Like in English, 첫사랑 often brings up nostalgia: school days, a crush you never confessed to, or a sweet relationship that ended.
There is a well-known Korean saying, 첫사랑은 이루어지지 않는다, "first love never works out," which many dramas love to prove wrong.
Use it for the person too: 그 사람이 내 첫사랑이야, "That person is my first love."

forms.en: To fall in love at first sight

forms.note: 첫 can go before many nouns.

examples.context: A romantic moment with a partner
Hearing an old song
examples.en: It makes me think of my first love.

examples.context: Getting to know someone

faq.q: Is cheotsarang one word?
faq.a: Yes. 첫사랑 is written as one word, though 첫 is written separately before most other nouns, like 첫 키스.

faq.q: Does cheotsarang mean the person or the feeling?
faq.a: Both. It can mean the experience of first love or the person you first loved.

meaning: I love it / I like it so much
intro: 너무 좋아 (neomu joa) means "I love it," "I like it so much" or "it's so good" in Korean. It is a casual, happy reaction to food, music, weather, a gift or a person.
literal: 너무 (neomu) means "so" or "too," and 좋아 (joa) is the casual form of 좋다, "to be good." So it is literally "(it is) so good."
usage: 너무 used to mean only "too much," with a negative feel. Today it is normal, and officially accepted, to use it for positive things too, so 너무 좋아 just means "so good."
좋다 is an adjective. When a person is the subject, like 네가 너무 좋아, it means "I like you so much." This is a little different from 좋아해, which is the verb "to like."
Add 요 to be polite: 너무 좋아요. For even more excitement, people say 진짜 너무 좋아.

forms.note: Plain form; often said to yourself.

examples.context: Listening to a new song with a friend
Telling a partner how you feel
Stepping outside on a spring day

faq.q: What is the difference between neomu joa and joahae?
faq.a: 좋아 comes from the adjective 좋다, "to be good," so 너무 좋아 is "it's so good" or, about a person, "I like you so much." 좋아해 is the verb "to like" and focuses on your feeling for someone or something.

faq.q: Doesn't neomu mean "too much"?
faq.a: It originally did, but today 너무 is used for positive things too, and it is officially accepted that way. 너무 좋아 is completely natural.

intro: 심쿵 (simkung) is Korean slang for the moment your heart skips a beat, usually because someone is cute, attractive or sweet. Fans use it about idols, and people use it about a crush's smile or a romantic drama scene.
literal: It is short for 심장이 쿵, from 심장 (simjang), "heart," and 쿵 (kung), a "thud" sound. So it is literally "heart goes thud."
usage: It is playful internet and spoken slang, popular with young people. Use it with friends, in fan comments and in texts, not in formal settings.
Add 하다 to make it a verb: 심쿵했어, "my heart skipped a beat." 심쿵사 is a joke word meaning "died from heart-flutter."
A related, more standard word is 설레다, to feel a flutter of excitement, as in 설레 ("I'm all fluttery").

forms.en: To have your heart skip a beat

forms.note: Standard word for a similar feeling.

examples.context: After a crush smiles at you
examples.en: My heart just skipped a beat.

examples.context: Commenting on an idol's photo
Telling a friend about your idol

faq.q: Is simkung a real Korean word?
faq.a: It is slang, not a dictionary word, but almost every young Korean knows it. It comes from 심장 (heart) and 쿵 (thud).

faq.q: Can I say simkung to my crush?
faq.a: Yes, in a playful way, like 방금 심쿵했어. It is light and flirty, not heavy.

intro: 주세요 (juseyo) means "please give me" in Korean. You put it after the thing you want, so 물 주세요 means "water, please." It is the word you will use most when ordering food, shopping or asking for help.
literal: It comes from the verb 주다 (juda), "to give," plus the polite request ending 세요. So it literally means "please give."
usage: Say the item first and 주세요 last: 이거 주세요 (this one, please), 커피 주세요 (coffee, please). It is polite enough for shops, restaurants, taxis and strangers.
주세요 also attaches to verbs to mean "please do this for me." 도와주세요 is "please help me" and 기다려 주세요 is "please wait."
With friends, the casual version is 줘 (jwo). In very formal settings, such as announcements, you will hear 주십시오.

forms.note: Formal, used in announcements and notices.
Verb + 주세요 asks someone to do something for you.

examples.context: Ordering at a café
Pointing at something in a shop
Asking a server at a restaurant

faq.q: How do you say please in Korean?
faq.a: Korean does not have one word for "please." When asking for something, you add 주세요 after it, like 물 주세요 (water, please). 좀 softens a request further.

faq.q: What is the difference between juseyo and jebal?
faq.a: 주세요 is the everyday "please give me" for ordering and asking. 제발 is a pleading "please, I beg you" used when you really want something.

faq.q: Is juseyo rude?
faq.a: No. It is polite and fine with strangers and staff. Only with someone much older or in a formal setting might you choose 주시겠어요 to sound softer.

intro: 맛있어요 (masisseoyo) means "it's delicious" or "it tastes good" in Korean. It is the polite form, so you can say it to anyone, from a restaurant owner to a friend's parents. With a rising tone, 맛있어요? asks "Is it good?"
literal: 맛 means taste or flavor and 있어요 means "there is" or "has." So it literally says "it has taste," which in Korean means it tastes good. The opposite is 맛없어요 (madeopseoyo), "it has no taste," meaning it's not good.
usage: Koreans say it a lot while eating, especially to the person who cooked or paid. Telling a host 정말 맛있어요 is a kind and expected compliment.
With friends, drop the 요 and say 맛있어. 맛있다! (plain form) is what people often say to themselves after the first bite.
Learners sometimes say 맛있어요 about a person, but it only describes food and drink. For a good-looking person, use 멋있어요 (cool) or 예뻐요 (pretty).

forms.note: Plain form, often said to yourself.
Formal, for speeches or very polite settings.
What staff or hosts say when serving food.

examples.context: Taking the first bite at a friend's home
Asking a friend about their dish
Complimenting a grandmother's cooking
examples.en: Grandma, your kimchi is truly delicious.

faq.q: How do you pronounce masisseoyo?
faq.a: Most people say it like "ma-shi-sseo-yo." The ㅅ before ㅣ sounds close to "sh," which is why many people spell it mashisoyo.

faq.q: How do you say "it's not delicious" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 맛없어요 (madeopseoyo). It can sound blunt, so people often soften it with 좀 별로예요 (it's not great).

faq.q: What do you say after a meal in Korean?
faq.a: Say 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeosseumnida), "I ate well," to thank the cook or whoever paid.

intro: 얼마예요 (eolmayeyo) means "How much is it?" in Korean. It is the polite question you use in shops, markets and taxis to ask a price. Point at something and say 이거 얼마예요? (How much is this?)
literal: 얼마 means "how much" and 예요 is the polite form of "is." Put together it says "How much is (it)?"
usage: It is polite, so it works with any shop owner or stranger. In traditional markets you will often hear it followed by a request for a small discount.
With friends you can say 얼마야? (casual). In formal settings, such as at a counter in a hotel, 얼마입니까? also works.
Koreans often write it wrongly as 얼마에요. The standard spelling is 얼마예요, because 얼마 ends in a vowel.

forms.en: How much is it all together?

examples.context: Pointing at a scarf at a market stall
At the checkout with several items
examples.en: How much is it all together?

examples.context: Buying fruit at a market

faq.q: Is it eolmayeyo or eolmaeyo?
faq.a: The correct spelling is 얼마예요. After a word ending in a vowel, the polite "is" becomes 예요, so 얼마에요 is a common mistake.

faq.q: How do you understand the answer?
faq.a: Prices are usually given in Sino-Korean numbers plus 원 (won), for example 만 원 (10,000 won). If you are lost, ask them to show you on a calculator or phone.

intro: 안녕히 가세요 (annyeonghi gaseyo) means "goodbye" in Korean, said to someone who is leaving. You say it when you stay and the other person goes. If you are the one leaving, say 안녕히 계세요 instead.
literal: 안녕히 means "in peace" or "safely," and 가세요 is a polite way to say "go." So it literally means "go in peace."
usage: The choice depends on who is moving. Shop staff say 안녕히 가세요 to customers walking out, and a host says it to guests at the door.
If both people are leaving, for example parting on the street, both can say 안녕히 가세요.
It is polite, so it works with strangers, teachers and older people. With friends, say 잘 가 (jal ga) or just 안녕.

forms.note: Formal, heard from staff and announcers.
A warm alternative, often at night.
The version for the person leaving.

examples.context: A shop owner to a customer walking out
Students as their teacher leaves the classroom
A host closing a live stream

faq.q: What is the difference between annyeonghi gaseyo and annyeonghi gyeseyo?
