faq.a: 안녕히 가세요 (go in peace) is said to the person leaving. 안녕히 계세요 (stay in peace) is said by the person leaving to the one who stays.

faq.q: Can I say annyeonghi gaseyo to a friend?
faq.a: You can, but it sounds stiff. Friends usually say 잘 가 or 안녕.

faq.q: What do you say on the phone?
faq.a: Both people are staying put, so many people simply say 네, 들어가세요 or 안녕히 계세요. 안녕히 가세요 is less common on the phone.

intro: 안녕히 계세요 (annyeonghi gyeseyo) means "goodbye" in Korean, said by the person who is leaving to the person who stays. Say it when you walk out of a shop, a classroom or someone's home.
literal: 안녕히 means "in peace" or "safely," and 계세요 is the respectful form of 있다, "to stay" or "to be." So it literally means "stay in peace."
usage: Think about who is staying. You are leaving and the shopkeeper stays, so you say 안녕히 계세요 and they answer 안녕히 가세요.
It is polite and safe with anyone older or unfamiliar. With friends, the casual version is 잘 있어 (stay well).
Many people also say 수고하세요 when leaving a shop. It is common, but some feel it sounds odd toward someone older, so 안녕히 계세요 is the safer choice.

forms.note: Common when leaving a shop or office.
The reply you will hear back.

examples.context: Leaving a convenience store
Leaving the teacher's office
Wrapping up a visit at a friend's parents' home

faq.q: When do I say annyeonghi gyeseyo instead of annyeonghi gaseyo?
faq.a: Say 안녕히 계세요 when you are the one leaving. Say 안녕히 가세요 when the other person is leaving.

faq.q: What is the base form of gyeseyo?
faq.a: 계세요 comes from 계시다, the honorific verb for "to be" or "to stay" used for people you respect.

intro: 반갑습니다 (bangapseumnida) means "nice to meet you" or "glad to see you" in Korean. It is the formal form, used when meeting someone for the first time, at work or in front of a group. The full phrase 만나서 반갑습니다 means "nice to meet you."
literal: It comes from the adjective 반갑다 (bangapda), "to be glad or happy to see someone," plus the formal ending 습니다. So it literally says "I am glad (to see you)."
usage: Use it at introductions, business meetings and when greeting an audience. It often follows 안녕하세요 and your name.
Unlike "nice to meet you," it is not only for first meetings. You can also say it warmly to someone you have not seen in a while.
For a slightly softer polite version, say 반가워요. With friends or younger people, say 반가워.

forms.note: Very polite, only for a first meeting.

examples.context: Meeting a new coworker
A speaker greeting the audience
examples.en: It's good to see you, everyone.

examples.context: Replying to someone who greeted you first

faq.q: How do you reply to bangapseumnida?
faq.a: Say 저도 반갑습니다 (jeodo bangapseumnida), "nice to meet you too."

faq.q: What is the difference between bangapseumnida and bangawoyo?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. 반갑습니다 is formal, and 반가워요 is polite but softer and more friendly.

intro: 반가워 (bangawo) means "nice to meet you" or "good to see you" in Korean. It is casual, so you say it to friends, people your age or younger. It shows you are happy to see someone.
literal: It comes from 반갑다 (bangapda), "to be glad to see someone." 반가워 is its casual present form.
usage: Use it with classmates, friends of friends and younger people. For someone older or a stranger, use 반가워요 or 반갑습니다.
It works for first meetings and for seeing someone after a long time. 반갑다! said on its own sounds like "so good to see you!"
Idols sometimes say 반가워 to fans in a friendly way, but in daily life it is not for people above you.

examples.context: Meeting a friend's friend
Replying to a new classmate
Running into an old friend

faq.q: Can I say bangawo to someone older?
faq.a: Not usually. Use 반가워요 or 반갑습니다 with anyone older or unfamiliar.

faq.q: How do you reply to bangawo?
faq.a: Say 나도 반가워 (nado bangawo), "nice to meet you too."

intro: 생일 축하해 (saengil chukhae) means "happy birthday" in Korean. It is the casual form for friends, siblings and partners. For someone older, say 생일 축하해요 or 생일 축하드려요.
literal: 생일 means birthday and 축하해 means "I congratulate." Together it says "congratulations on your birthday."
usage: Koreans send it by text first thing in the morning or at midnight. Close friends often shorten it to 생축 or ㅊㅋ in chats.
The Korean birthday song uses the formal form: 생일 축하합니다, 생일 축하합니다, 사랑하는 (name)의 생일 축하합니다.
For parents or grandparents, many people use the honorific word 생신 (birthday) and say 생신 축하드려요.

forms.note: Very respectful, for teachers or bosses.

examples.context: Texting a best friend at midnight
Calling a younger sibling's name
A card for mom

faq.q: How do you say happy birthday politely in Korean?
faq.a: Say 생일 축하해요 (polite) or 생일 축하드려요 (very respectful). For elders, use 생신 축하드려요.

faq.q: How do you reply to saengil chukhae?
faq.a: Say 고마워 (thanks) to a friend or 감사합니다 to someone older.

intro: 축하해 (chukhae) means "congratulations" or "congrats" in Korean. It is the casual form, for friends and people younger than you. Put the occasion in front of it, like 합격 축하해, "congrats on passing."
literal: 축하 is a Sino-Korean word meaning celebration or congratulations, and 해 is the casual form of 하다, "to do." So it means "I congratulate (you)."
usage: Use it for good news of any kind: passing an exam, a new job, a wedding, a birthday or a win.
With someone older, say 축하해요 or 축하드려요. In speeches and on stage you will hear 축하합니다 or 축하드립니다.
In texts, people type ㅊㅋ or ㅊㅋㅊㅋ as a quick, playful congrats between friends.

forms.note: Very respectful, for elders and bosses.

examples.context: A friend passed a big exam
Texting a friend who got a job
Congratulating a coworker on their wedding

faq.q: Is it chukha or chukhae?
faq.a: The casual form is 축하해, so chukhae is more accurate. Chukha is a common shortened search spelling.

faq.q: How do you say congratulations formally?
faq.a: Say 축하합니다 (chukhahamnida) or, even more respectfully, 축하드립니다 (chukhadeurimnida).

intro: 실례합니다 (sillyehamnida) means "excuse me" in Korean. It is a formal, polite phrase you say before interrupting someone, entering a room or doing something that might bother them. It sounds respectful and a little formal.
literal: 실례 is a Sino-Korean word meaning "a breach of manners," and 합니다 is the formal form of 하다, "to do." So it literally says "I am being rude," as an apology in advance.
usage: Say it when knocking on an office door, calling someone late at night, or starting to talk to a stranger. 실례지만 ("excuse me, but") is used before a question.
To get past people in a crowded bus or subway, Koreans usually say 잠시만요 or 잠깐만요 instead. To call a server, say 저기요 or 여기요.
After you have caused a bother, the past form 실례했습니다 means "sorry for the trouble."

forms.note: Used before asking a stranger something.

examples.context: Knocking on a teacher's office door
Calling someone late in the evening
examples.en: Sorry to bother you so late.

examples.context: Stepping out of a meeting briefly

faq.q: How do I say excuse me to get past someone?
faq.a: Say 잠시만요 or 잠깐만요. 실례합니다 also works but is more formal.

faq.q: Is sillyehamnida the same as sorry?
faq.a: Not quite. 실례합니다 is said before or while you bother someone. For a real apology, use 죄송합니다.

intro: 죄송합니다 (joesonghamnida) means "I'm sorry" in Korean. It is the formal, respectful apology you use with customers, bosses, teachers, elders and strangers. It is stronger and more polite than 미안합니다.
literal: 죄송 is a Sino-Korean word for feeling at fault and ashamed, and 합니다 is the formal ending of 하다. So it means "I feel at fault" or "I am sorry."
usage: Use it whenever you apologize to someone above you or to someone you do not know. Staff say it to customers, and students say it to teachers.
죄송해요 is the polite but softer version, common in everyday speech. 미안해 is only for friends, family and younger people.
Adding 정말 (really) or 진심으로 (sincerely) makes the apology deeper. A small bow usually goes with it.

forms.note: Formal but less humble; often to equals or juniors.

examples.context: Arriving late to a meeting
A store clerk to a customer
Bumping into an older stranger

faq.q: What is the difference between joesonghamnida and mianhamnida?
faq.a: Both mean "I'm sorry." 죄송합니다 is humbler and is the right choice for elders, bosses and customers. 미안합니다 is used more with equals or people younger than you.

faq.q: How do you reply to joesonghamnida?
faq.a: Say 괜찮아요 (it's okay) or 괜찮습니다 (formal).

intro: 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeosseumnida) means "I ate well" and is how Koreans say "thank you for the meal" after eating. You say it to whoever cooked or paid. Its partner phrase, 잘 먹겠습니다, is said before eating.
literal: 잘 means "well," and 먹었습니다 is the formal past form of 먹다, "to eat." So it literally says "I ate well."
usage: Say it when you finish a meal at someone's home, when a boss or senior pays for dinner, or as you leave a small restaurant.
It is formal and respectful. With family or friends, 잘 먹었어요 (polite) or 잘 먹었어 (casual) is common.
To thank the person who paid, you can add 덕분에 (thanks to you): 덕분에 잘 먹었습니다.

forms.en: Thanks to you, I ate well

examples.context: Finishing dinner at a friend's parents' home
examples.en: Thank you, that was a wonderful meal.

examples.context: Leaving a restaurant, to the owner
After a senior treated you to lunch

faq.q: What is the difference between jal meokgesseumnida and jal meogeosseumnida?
faq.a: 잘 먹겠습니다 (I will eat well) is said before the meal. 잘 먹었습니다 (I ate well) is said after.

faq.q: Do I say it at a restaurant?
faq.a: Many people say it to the owner at small, family-run restaurants as they leave. At big chain restaurants a simple 감사합니다 is enough.

intro: 다녀오겠습니다 (danyeo ogesseumnida) means "I'll be back" or "I'm heading out" in Korean. People say it when leaving home for school or work. The family usually answers 다녀와 or 잘 다녀와, "see you later."
literal: It comes from 다녀오다, "to go somewhere and come back," plus 겠, which shows intention, and the formal ending 습니다. So it says "I will go and come back."
usage: It is the classic thing children say to parents when leaving the house. In dramas you will hear it at the front door every morning.
Many families use the softer 다녀올게요 (polite) or 다녀올게 (casual) in everyday life. The formal 다녀오겠습니다 sounds proper and well brought up.
When you come home, say 다녀왔습니다, "I'm back." The family replies 왔어? or 잘 다녀왔어?

forms.note: Polite reply to the person leaving.

examples.context: Leaving for school in the morning
Saying goodbye to mom at the door
Heading to work

faq.q: How do you reply to danyeo ogesseumnida?
faq.a: Family usually says 잘 다녀와 (casual) or 다녀오세요 (polite), meaning "have a good day" or "see you later."

faq.q: What do you say when you come home?
faq.a: Say 다녀왔습니다 (danyeo wasseumnida), "I'm back."

intro: 어서 오세요 (eoseo oseyo) means "welcome" in Korean. It is what shop staff call out when a customer walks in, and what hosts say to guests at the door. It is polite and warm.
literal: 어서 means "quickly" or "come on," and 오세요 is a polite way to say "come." So it literally says "please come in, come on in."
usage: You will hear it in almost every café, restaurant and convenience store. Customers do not need to say it back. A nod or 안녕하세요 is enough.
Hosts also say it to guests arriving at home. Friends say the casual 어서 와 (come on in).
In big stores and hotels you may hear the more formal 어서 오십시오.

forms.note: Formal, used by staff in hotels and big stores.

examples.context: Staff greeting a customer at a café
Welcoming grandma at the front door
A host opening an event

faq.q: How do you reply to eoseo oseyo?
faq.a: You do not have to. In shops people usually just nod or say 안녕하세요.

faq.q: What is the casual form?
faq.a: 어서 와 (eoseo wa), "come on in," for friends and family.

intro: 여보세요 (yeoboseyo) means "hello?" when answering or starting a phone call in Korean. It is only for the phone, not for greeting someone face to face. For a normal hello, use 안녕하세요.
literal: It is usually traced to 여보, an old way of calling someone's attention, roughly "hey there" or "look here," plus the polite ending 세요.
usage: People say it when picking up, and again if the line goes quiet or breaks up, like "Hello? Are you there?"
In person, it can be used to get a stranger's attention, but it sounds a bit sharp or old-fashioned. 저기요 is the more common choice.
Do not mix it up with 여보 (yeobo), which married couples call each other, like "honey."

examples.context: Answering a call
The connection is bad
Calling mom

faq.q: Can I say yeoboseyo instead of annyeonghaseyo?
faq.a: No. 여보세요 is for phone calls. Face to face, say 안녕하세요.

faq.q: Is yeoboseyo related to yeobo?
faq.a: They share a root in an old way of calling someone, but today they are different words. 여보 means "honey" between spouses, and 여보세요 is the phone hello.

intro: 빨리 (ppalli) means "quickly" or "hurry" in Korean. Said on its own, 빨리! is a casual "hurry up!" It is also an everyday word in any sentence that needs "fast."
literal: It is the adverb form of 빠르다 (ppareuda), "to be fast."
usage: 빨리 alone or doubled as 빨리빨리 is a casual command to hurry, used with friends, family and children.
The word itself fits any level of politeness. Add a polite verb to use it with anyone: 빨리 오세요 (please come quickly).
빨리빨리 is also known as a nickname for Korea's fast-paced culture: quick delivery, quick service and little patience for waiting.

examples.context: Calling a friend who is running late
A parent rushing kids out the door
Asking someone to come urgently

faq.q: What does ppalli ppalli mean?
faq.a: It means "hurry, hurry" and is also used to describe Korean culture's love of speed and efficiency.

faq.q: Is ppalli rude?
faq.a: The word is neutral. Saying 빨리! as a command is casual, so with older people use 빨리 와 주세요 or a softer phrase.

intro: 뭐 해 (mwohae) means "What are you doing?" in Korean. It is casual and very common in texts between friends and couples, much like "wyd?" or "what are you up to?"
literal: 뭐 is the short, spoken form of 무엇, "what," and 해 is the casual form of 하다, "to do." So it says "what (are you) doing?" The dictionary spelling has a space, but people often type 뭐해.
usage: As a text, 뭐 해? is a friendly check-in that often means "I want to talk" or "are you free?"
Said sharply, it can mean "What are you doing?!" when someone is doing something odd. 뭐 하는 거야? is the stronger, more annoyed version.
With someone older, use 뭐 해요? or the respectful 뭐 하세요?

forms.en: What are you up to right now?
What do you think you're doing?

forms.note: Often heard from parents or teachers.

examples.context: Texting a crush at night
examples.en: What are you doing right now?

examples.context: Making weekend plans
examples.en: What are you doing this weekend?

examples.context: Catching a sibling eating your snacks

faq.q: Is it mwohae or mwo hae?
faq.a: Both are seen. The standard spelling is 뭐 해 with a space, but 뭐해 is very common in texts.

faq.q: How do you answer mwohae?
faq.a: Say what you are doing, or just 그냥 있어 (just hanging out) or 아무것도 안 해 (nothing).

intro: 밥 먹었어 (bap meogeosseo) means "Did you eat?" in Korean. As a question, it is a caring, everyday greeting, close to "How are you?" Said as a statement, it means "I ate."
literal: 밥 means cooked rice and, more broadly, a meal. 먹었어 is the casual past form of 먹다, "to eat." So it literally asks "Did you eat rice?"
usage: Koreans ask it to show they care, so you do not need to give a detailed answer. 응, 먹었어 (yeah, I ate) or 아직 (not yet) is enough.
It is casual, for friends, partners and family. With older people, use 식사하셨어요? (Did you have your meal?) or 밥 먹었어요? with someone a bit older.
If someone says 아직 (not yet), the natural next line is 밥 먹자! (Let's eat!)

forms.note: Friendly, often not a firm plan.

examples.context: Texting a friend at lunchtime
Calling mom after work
Answering the question

faq.q: Why do Koreans ask if you ate?
faq.a: It is a way of showing care, a bit like "How are you?" It comes from times when having enough food was not guaranteed.

faq.q: How do you say it to someone older?
faq.a: Say 식사하셨어요? (siksahasyeosseoyo). For grandparents, 진지 잡수셨어요? is the most respectful.

intro: 잘 지냈어요 (jal jinaesseoyo) means "How have you been?" in Korean when said as a question. It is the polite way to greet someone you have not seen for a while. Said as a statement, it means "I've been well."
literal: 잘 means "well," and 지냈어요 is the polite past form of 지내다, "to get along" or "to live (day to day)." So it literally means "Did you get along well?"
usage: Use it when you meet someone after weeks, months or years. It often comes with 오랜만이에요 (long time no see).
The answer uses the same words: 네, 잘 지냈어요 (yes, I've been well). Then ask back with 잘 지냈어요?
With friends, say 잘 지냈어? With someone older or a boss, the respectful 잘 지내셨어요? is better.

forms.note: Present tense, also used as a goodbye.

forms.en: How have you been all this time?

examples.context: Meeting an old classmate
examples.en: How have you been all this time?

examples.context: Answering the question
Greeting a coworker back from a long trip

faq.q: How do you answer jal jinaesseoyo?
faq.a: Say 네, 잘 지냈어요 (yes, I've been well) and ask back: 잘 지냈어요?

faq.q: What is the difference between jal jinaesseoyo and jal jinaeyo?
faq.a: 잘 지냈어요 is past tense, "have you been well?" 잘 지내요 is present, "I'm doing well," and is also a way to say "take care" when parting.

intro: 힘내 (himnae) is a casual Korean phrase that means "Cheer up!", "Hang in there!" or "Stay strong!". You say it to encourage someone who is tired, stressed or going through something hard.
literal: It comes from 힘내다, made of 힘 (strength, energy) and 내다 (to bring out). So it literally means "bring out your strength".
usage: Say 힘내 to a friend before an exam, after a breakup, or when they are worn out from work. It is warm and supportive, and it is very common in texts too.
힘내 is casual (banmal), so use it with friends, siblings and people younger than you. For someone older or someone you don't know well, say 힘내세요, which is polite and still sounds kind.
It is close to 화이팅 (fighting), but 화이팅 is more of a pep-talk cheer before a challenge, while 힘내 often carries sympathy for someone who is already struggling.

forms.note: Polite form for people you are not close to.
Polite and warm. Safe for elders, customers and coworkers.
Includes yourself, as in "let's both keep going".
Common one-word text to a friend.

examples.context: A friend is nervous about a test
examples.en: You can do it, hang in there!

examples.context: Saying goodbye to a coworker on a busy morning
Comforting a friend going through the same tough time

faq.q: What is the difference between himnae and hwaiting?
faq.a: Both encourage someone. 화이팅 is an upbeat cheer before a challenge, while 힘내 is gentler and often comforts someone who is already having a hard time.

faq.q: How do you say himnae politely?
faq.a: Say 힘내세요 (himnaeseyo). It is polite and kind, so you can say it to older people or people you don't know well.

faq.q: Is himnae rude?
faq.a: No, but it is casual. With elders or at work, 힘내세요 is the better choice.

intro: 기다려 (gidaryeo) means "Wait!" or "Wait for me" in casual Korean. It is the banmal form of 기다리다 (to wait), so you say it to friends, family or anyone younger than you.
literal: It is 기다리다 (to wait) with the casual ending 어, which merges into 기다려.
usage: Use 기다려 when you want someone to hold on, for example when a friend is walking ahead or you need a minute to get ready. Said sharply, it can sound like an order, so a softer 잠깐만 기다려 (wait just a moment) is common.
With people you are not close to, use 기다려 주세요 (please wait). Shop staff and receptionists say 잠시만 기다려 주세요 (please wait a moment) all the time.
기다려 is also the word Korean dog owners use for the command "Stay!". And 기다릴게 means "I'll wait", which is a very common line in romantic scenes.

forms.note: Casual request, softer than plain 기다려.
A promise, common in texts and love stories.

examples.context: A friend walks ahead of you
A clerk checking something for a customer
Thanking a friend who waited for you

faq.q: How do you say wait politely in Korean?
faq.a: Say 기다려 주세요 (please wait) or 잠시만 기다려 주세요 (please wait a moment).

faq.q: What is the difference between gidaryeo and jamkkanman?
faq.a: 잠깐만 means "just a moment" or "hold on". 기다려 is the verb "wait". People often combine them: 잠깐만 기다려.

faq.q: What does gidarilge mean?
faq.a: 기다릴게 means "I'll wait" or "I'll wait for you". It is casual and often sounds caring or romantic.

intro: 도와주세요 (dowajuseyo) means "Please help me" or "Help!" in polite Korean. You can use it to ask a stranger for a hand, or shout it in an emergency.
literal: It comes from 돕다 (to help) and 주다 (to give), which together make 도와주다 (to help someone out). The ending 세요 makes it a polite request.
usage: 도와주세요 is polite, so it works with strangers, shop staff, teachers and anyone older. Adding 좀 makes it softer: 좀 도와주세요 is like "Could you help me, please?"
In a real emergency people shout 도와주세요! or 살려 주세요! (Save me!). The emergency number in Korea is 119 for fire and ambulance and 112 for police.
With close friends, the casual form is 도와줘 (help me). Using 도와줘 with an older stranger would sound too familiar.

forms.note: Shouted in danger. Literally "please let me live".

examples.context: Asking a passerby for a hand with heavy bags
Calling out when someone has fallen
Asking a staff member about a ticket machine
examples.en: Could you help me with this?

faq.q: How do you say help in Korean?
faq.a: Say 도와주세요 (dowajuseyo) to ask for help politely. In danger, people also shout 살려 주세요 (Save me!).

faq.q: What is the casual form of dowajuseyo?
faq.a: 도와줘 (dowajwo). Use it only with friends, family or people younger than you.

faq.q: Is dowajuseyo one word or two?
faq.a: Both spellings are seen. 도와주다 is listed as one word in the dictionary, so 도와주세요 is standard, but 도와 주세요 with a space is also common.

meaning: I don't know / I'm not sure
intro: 모르겠어요 (moreugesseoyo) means "I don't know" or "I'm not sure" in polite Korean. It sounds softer than a flat "I don't know", more like "I'm not really sure".
literal: It is 모르다 (to not know) plus 겠, which here softens the statement, and the polite ending 어요.
usage: Use 모르겠어요 when you are asked something you can't answer, when you are confused, or when you can't decide. 잘 모르겠어요 (I'm not quite sure) is one of the most useful phrases for learners.
몰라요 also means "I don't know", but it is more blunt and factual. 모르겠어요 sounds more thoughtful and polite, so it is the safer choice with strangers, teachers and coworkers.
With friends, use 모르겠어 or the even shorter 몰라. In formal settings such as work meetings, 모르겠습니다 is used.

forms.note: Formal, for work or official settings.

examples.context: A stranger asks you for directions
A coworker asks if the meeting moved
Lost in a new neighborhood

faq.q: What is the difference between moreugesseoyo and mollayo?
faq.a: Both mean "I don't know". 모르겠어요 is softer and sounds like "I'm not sure", while 몰라요 is more direct.

faq.q: How do you say I don't understand in Korean?
faq.a: 모르겠어요 often covers it, as in 잘 모르겠어요. To say you didn't understand what someone said, 이해가 안 돼요 (I don't understand) is also common.

faq.q: What is the casual form?
faq.a: 모르겠어 or 몰라. Use them with friends and people younger than you.

intro: 알겠습니다 (algesseumnida) means "Understood", "Got it" or "Yes, I'll do that" in formal Korean. It is what you say when a boss, teacher or customer asks you to do something.
literal: It comes from 알다 (to know) plus 겠 and the formal ending 습니다. Together they mean "I understand" or "I will take that on board".
usage: You hear 알겠습니다 constantly at work, in the army, in shops and in any formal setting. It is often paired with 네: 네, 알겠습니다 (Yes, understood).
알겠어요 is the polite everyday version, and 알겠어 or 알았어 is casual for friends. Saying a casual form to your boss would sound careless.
Tone matters. A bright 알겠습니다 sounds willing, but a flat, clipped one can hint that the speaker is annoyed but going along with it.

forms.note: The standard reply to an instruction.
Extra respectful, often after an explanation.

examples.context: Replying to a manager's request
Accepting a task at work
examples.en: Understood, I'll do it right away

examples.context: After a teacher explains the homework

faq.q: What is the difference between algesseumnida and arasseo?
faq.a: Both mean "got it". 알겠습니다 is formal for work and elders, while 알았어 is casual for friends.

faq.q: Should I say algesseumnida or arasseumnida?
faq.a: At work and in formal replies, 알겠습니다 is the usual choice. 알았습니다 is also correct, but 알겠습니다 sounds more natural when accepting an instruction.

faq.q: How do you say okay politely in Korean?
faq.a: 네, 알겠습니다 for formal situations or 네, 알겠어요 for polite everyday ones.

intro: 좋은 아침 (joeun achim) means "Good morning" in Korean. It is a friendly, casual greeting, especially popular in texts and among friends and coworkers.
literal: 좋은 means "good" (from 좋다) and 아침 means "morning". It is a direct translation of the English greeting, and Koreans traditionally greet each other in the morning with 안녕하세요 instead.
usage: 좋은 아침 feels bright and a little modern. Friends text it to each other, couples say it, and coworkers in relaxed offices use it. Some people even say 굿모닝 straight from English.
For elders or formal settings, 안녕하세요 or 안녕히 주무셨어요? (Did you sleep well?) is more natural. You can make 좋은 아침 polite as 좋은 아침이에요 or 좋은 아침입니다, but it still sounds casual and cheerful.
A very common morning question between friends and family is 잘 잤어? (Did you sleep well?), which works like "good morning" too.

forms.note: Formal, sometimes used by presenters or in group chats at work.
Borrowed from English, casual and playful.

examples.context: Texting a friend first thing
Walking into a friendly office
A partner waking up
examples.en: Good morning, did you sleep well?

faq.q: How do you say good morning in Korean?
faq.a: 좋은 아침 is the direct way. Many Koreans simply say 안녕하세요, and to elders 안녕히 주무셨어요? (Did you sleep well?).

faq.q: Is joeun achim polite?
faq.a: It is friendly and casual. 좋은 아침이에요 adds politeness, but for elders 안녕하세요 is safer.

faq.q: Do Koreans actually say joeun achim?
faq.a: Yes, especially younger people, in texts and in relaxed workplaces. It is newer than 안녕하세요, which is still the default greeting.

intro: 잘 가 (jal ga) means "Bye!" or "Get home safe" in casual Korean. You say it to a friend who is leaving while you stay or go a different way.
literal: 잘 means "well" and 가 is the casual form of 가다 (to go), so it literally means "go well".
usage: Use 잘 가 with friends, siblings and younger people at the end of a hangout, a phone call or a chat. It often comes with 내일 봐 (see you tomorrow) or 조심히 가 (go safely).
The polite version is 안녕히 가세요, said to someone who is leaving. If you are the one leaving and the other person stays, say 잘 있어 (casual) or 안녕히 계세요 (polite) instead.
In emotional scenes, 잘 가 can also be a final goodbye, the way "farewell" works in English.

forms.note: Polite, to someone who is leaving.
Said by the person who is leaving.

examples.context: Parting at the subway station
A friend heads home late at night
Saying bye after dinner
examples.en: Bye, text me when you get there

faq.q: What is the difference between jal ga and jal isseo?
faq.a: 잘 가 is said to the person leaving. 잘 있어 is said by the person leaving to the one who stays.

faq.q: Is jal ga polite?
faq.a: No, it is casual. Use 안녕히 가세요 for elders and strangers, or 잘 가요 for a friendly polite version.

faq.q: Can jal ga mean goodbye forever?
faq.a: It can in sad or dramatic moments, but day to day it just means "bye, get home safe".

intro: 또 만나요 (tto mannayo) means "See you again" or "Let's meet again" in polite Korean. It is a warm way to say goodbye when you hope to see someone again.
literal: 또 means "again" and 만나요 is the polite form of 만나다 (to meet). So it literally means "meet again".
usage: Say 또 만나요 at the end of a pleasant first meeting, a class, or a chat with a shop owner you like. It is polite but friendly, not stiff.
Korean YouTubers and radio hosts often end with 다음에 또 만나요 (see you next time). With friends, the casual form is 또 만나 or, more often, 또 봐.
Depending on tone, it can be a goodbye or a real suggestion. Said with a smile and a question, 또 만나요? can mean "Shall we meet again?"

forms.note: Casual, the most common among friends.

examples.context: Ending a language exchange
A YouTuber signing off
examples.en: See you again in the next video!

examples.context: Leaving a class you enjoyed

faq.q: What is the difference between tto mannayo and tto bwayo?
faq.a: Both mean "see you again". 또 봐요 (literally "see again") is slightly more everyday, while 또 만나요 ("meet again") can sound a bit warmer or more deliberate.

faq.q: How do you say see you later in Korean?
faq.a: Casually, 나중에 봐 or 이따 봐 (see you in a bit). Politely, 다음에 또 만나요.

faq.q: Is tto mannayo formal?
faq.a: It is polite, not formal. It suits most everyday situations with people you are not close to.

intro: 천만에요 (cheonmaneyo) means "You're welcome" or "Not at all" in polite Korean. It is the answer most textbooks teach after someone says thank you.
literal: 천만 means "ten million", and 천만에 is an old expression meaning "far from it" or "not at all". So the idea is "it was nothing at all".
usage: 천만에요 is correct and polite, but in daily life it can sound a little textbook-like or formal. Many Koreans reply to thanks with 아니에요 (not at all), 별말씀을요 (don't mention it), or a simple smile and 네.
Among friends, people usually say 뭘 or 아니야 instead. 천만에 on its own exists but is rare in casual talk.
It is still a perfectly safe phrase for learners. Nobody will find it rude, and it works well in shops, classes and with people you have just met.

forms.note: The most common everyday reply to thanks.

examples.context: Someone thanks you for holding the door
A classmate thanks you for your notes
A neighbor thanks you for helping
examples.en: You're welcome, I'm glad it helped

faq.q: How do you say you're welcome in Korean?
faq.a: 천만에요 is the textbook answer. In real conversations, 아니에요 and 별말씀을요 are very common too.

faq.q: Do Koreans actually say cheonmaneyo?
faq.a: Yes, but less often than textbooks suggest. It can sound slightly formal, so many people say 아니에요 instead.

faq.q: What does cheonman mean?
faq.a: 천만 means ten million. 천만에 is an old expression meaning "not at all" or "far from it".

intro: 좀 (jom) means "a little" or "a bit" in Korean, and it is also used like "please" to soften a request. It is one of the most common words in everyday speech.
literal: 좀 is a shortened form of 조금 (a little).
usage: As "a bit", 좀 works like English: 좀 더 (a bit more), 좀 비싸요 (it's a bit expensive). As a softener, you slip it into requests to sound gentler: 물 좀 주세요 (Could I have some water, please?).
Said on its own with an annoyed tone, 좀! means something like "Come on!" or "Seriously!", and 좀 그만해 means "Cut it out". So the feeling depends a lot on your voice.
좀 itself has no politeness level, so it fits with both polite and casual sentences. The ending of the sentence decides how polite you sound.

forms.note: The full form, a bit more careful or written.
Very common in shops and at meals.

examples.context: Asking a server for water
examples.en: Could I have some water, please?

examples.context: A parent at dinner
Texting a sibling for help

faq.q: Does jom mean please?
faq.a: Not exactly, but it softens a request in a way that feels like "please". 물 좀 주세요 is like "Some water, please".

faq.q: What is the difference between jom and jogeum?
faq.a: 좀 is the shortened, everyday form of 조금. Both mean "a little", but only 좀 is commonly used as a request softener.

faq.q: Is jom rude?
faq.a: No. It usually makes you sound softer. Only an irritated 좀! on its own sounds sharp.

intro: 뭐 (mwo) means "what" in Korean. It is the everyday spoken form of 무엇, and you will hear it in questions, surprised reactions, and even as a filler word.
literal: 뭐 is a shortened form of 무엇 (what), which sounds more formal or written.
usage: In questions, 뭐 is everywhere: 뭐 해? (What are you doing?), 뭐 먹을래? (What do you want to eat?). The politeness comes from the ending, so 뭐 해요? is polite and 뭐 해? is casual.
On its own, 뭐? means "What?" when you are surprised or didn't hear. Be careful: a sharp 뭐? to an older person sounds rude, so say 네? instead when you didn't catch something.
People also use 뭐 as a filler, a bit like "well" or "like": 뭐, 괜찮아 (Well, it's fine).

examples.context: Texting a friend in the evening
Deciding on dinner with a friend
examples.en: What do you want to eat?

examples.context: A host offering drinks
examples.en: What would you like to drink?

faq.q: What is the difference between mwo and mwoya?
faq.a: 뭐 is the word "what". 뭐야 adds the casual ending 야, so it means "What is it?" or works as a reaction like "What the...?"

faq.q: Is saying mwo rude?
faq.a: The word itself is not rude. But a sharp 뭐? to someone older sounds disrespectful, so use 네? when you didn't hear them.

faq.q: Why do Koreans say mwo so much?
faq.a: Besides meaning "what", it is a common filler like "well" or "like", so it shows up in many sentences.

intro: 어디 (eodi) means "where" in Korean. It is the word you use to ask where someone is, where something is, or where they are going.
literal: 어디 is a basic question word. Particles attach to it: 어디에 (at where), 어디서 (from where, at where), 어디로 (to where).
usage: 어디 itself has no politeness level, the ending does. 어디야? is casual, 어디예요? is polite, and 어디세요? is respectful, often used on the phone.
어디 가? can mean "Where are you going?" or "Are you going somewhere?" depending on intonation. Koreans often ask it as a friendly greeting without really needing the answer.
어디 아파? (Where does it hurt? / Are you sick?) and 어디 보자 (Let me see) are other common uses.

forms.note: Casual, very common in calls and texts.

forms.en: Where is it? / Where are you?

examples.context: Calling a friend who is late
Asking staff in a cafe
Seeing a friend with a suitcase

faq.q: How do you say where are you in Korean?
faq.a: Casually, 어디야? Politely, 어디예요? or, more respectfully, 어디세요?

faq.q: How do you ask where the bathroom is in Korean?
faq.a: 화장실이 어디예요? (Where is the restroom?)

faq.q: Is it eodi or odi?
faq.a: The Korean is 어디. The standard romanization is eodi, but many people type odi or uhdi.

intro: 고맙습니다 (gomapseumnida) means "Thank you" in formal Korean. It is just as polite as 감사합니다 and is used with strangers, elders and in public.
literal: It comes from 고맙다 (to be thankful), a native Korean word, with the formal ending 습니다. 감사합니다 comes from 감사 (gratitude), a word from Chinese characters.
usage: 고맙습니다 and 감사합니다 are both correct in formal situations. 감사합니다 is heard more often in business and service settings, while 고맙습니다 can feel a little warmer and more personal.
The polite everyday form is 고마워요, and the casual form for friends is 고마워. Using 고마워 with an elder would be too familiar.
Add 정말 (really) or 너무 (so) to make it stronger: 정말 고맙습니다.

forms.note: Casual, for friends and younger people.
Equally formal, very common in service settings.

examples.context: Thanking a stranger who returned your wallet
Receiving change at a market stall
Thanking an older neighbor for helping you move
examples.en: Thank you so much for helping me

faq.q: What is the difference between gomapseumnida and kamsahamnida?
faq.a: Both are formal "thank you". 감사합니다 uses a Chinese-origin word and is more common in business, while 고맙습니다 is native Korean and can sound a little warmer.

faq.q: Is gomapseumnida less polite than kamsahamnida?
faq.a: No. Both use the same formal ending and are equally polite.

faq.q: How do you reply to gomapseumnida?
faq.a: 아니에요 (not at all) or 천만에요 (you're welcome).

intro: 이름이 뭐예요? (ireumi mwoyeyo) means "What's your name?" in polite Korean. It is the standard way to ask someone's name when you meet them.
literal: 이름 means "name", 이 is the subject marker, 뭐 means "what", and 예요 is the polite "is". So it is literally "Name is what?"
usage: Use 이름이 뭐예요? with people around your age or younger whom you don't know well, such as at a class or a language exchange. With friends and children, the casual form is 이름이 뭐야?
For someone clearly older or in a formal setting, 성함이 어떻게 되세요? is much more respectful. 성함 is the honorific word for name.
A common spelling mistake is 뭐에요. The correct spelling is 뭐예요, because 뭐 ends in a vowel. To answer, say 제 이름은 ___이에요 (after a consonant) or ___예요 (after a vowel).

forms.note: Very respectful, for elders and formal settings.

examples.context: Meeting someone at a language exchange
Meeting a cute dog at the park
Gently asking a new classmate
examples.en: By any chance, what's your name?

faq.q: Is it mwoyeyo or mwoeyo?
faq.a: The correct spelling is 뭐예요. 뭐에요 is a very common mistake, even among Koreans.

faq.q: How do you ask an older person's name?
faq.a: Say 성함이 어떻게 되세요? It uses the honorific word 성함 and is much more respectful.

faq.q: How do I answer?
faq.a: Say 제 이름은 ___예요 if your name ends in a vowel (민지예요) or ___이에요 if it ends in a consonant (지민이에요). 저는 ___예요 also works.

intro: 행복해 (haengbokhae) means "I'm happy" in casual Korean. It describes a deep, warm happiness, the kind you feel with people you love or when life feels good.
literal: It comes from 행복 (happiness) and 하다, making 행복하다 (to be happy). The casual ending turns it into 행복해.
usage: Say 행복해 to friends, family or a partner when you feel truly happy or content. It also works as a question: 행복해? (Are you happy?).

행복하다 is about overall happiness. For being glad about one event, Koreans often say 기뻐 (I'm glad) or 좋아 (I love it, it's good). Saying 행복해 about a small thing, like good food, is fine but sounds playful or extra emotional.
The polite form is 행복해요. 행복하세요 (be happy) is a common warm wish on cards and at the end of letters.

forms.note: Dictionary form, also used in diaries and captions.
Warm wish, common in cards and messages.

examples.context: On a perfect day out with friends
A couple talking
examples.en: I'm happy when I'm with you

examples.context: Telling a coworker about your new life

faq.q: How do you say I'm happy in Korean?
faq.a: Casually, 행복해. Politely, 행복해요. For being glad about something specific, 기뻐요 also works.

faq.q: What is the difference between haengbokhae and gippeo?
faq.a: 행복해 is a deep, general happiness. 기뻐 (glad) is usually about a particular piece of good news.

faq.q: What does haengbokhaseyo mean?
faq.a: 행복하세요 means "Be happy" or "Wishing you happiness". It is a warm, polite wish.

intro: 피곤해 (pigonhae) means "I'm tired" in casual Korean. It describes being worn out or exhausted, physically or mentally.
literal: It comes from 피곤 (fatigue) and 하다, making 피곤하다 (to be tired). The casual ending gives 피곤해.
usage: Say 피곤해 with friends and family after a long day, a hard workout or a night of little sleep. With a rising tone, 피곤해? means "Are you tired?"
피곤해 is about being worn out. If you mean sleepy, say 졸려. People often say both: 피곤하고 졸려 (I'm tired and sleepy).
The polite form is 피곤해요. A caring thing to say to someone who looks worn out is 피곤해 보여 (You look tired) or 피곤하겠다 (You must be tired).

examples.context: Getting home after a long shift
Telling a coworker how you feel
Worrying about a friend

faq.q: What is the difference between pigonhae and jollyeo?
faq.a: 피곤해 means tired or worn out. 졸려 means sleepy. You can be tired without being sleepy.

faq.q: How do you say I'm tired politely?
faq.a: Say 피곤해요. In formal settings, 피곤합니다.

faq.q: How do you say you look tired in Korean?
faq.a: 피곤해 보여 (casual) or 피곤해 보여요 (polite).

intro: 아파 (apa) means "It hurts", "Ow" or "I'm sick" in casual Korean. You say it about pain in a body part or about feeling ill.
literal: It is the casual form of 아프다 (to hurt, to be sick). One word covers both pain and illness.
usage: Name the body part before it: 머리 아파 (my head hurts), 배 아파 (my stomach hurts), 목 아파 (my throat hurts). 어디 아파? means "Where does it hurt?" or "Are you sick?"
아파 can also describe emotional pain: 마음이 아파 (my heart aches) is common in sad scenes and songs. For a quick "ouch!" people often say 아야! or 아!
Don't mix it up with 아빠 (appa, dad). The polite form is 아파요, which you would use with a doctor or pharmacist.

forms.note: Polite form, e.g. at the doctor.

forms.en: Where does it hurt? / Are you sick?

forms.note: Also used for "this is a headache" situations.

examples.context: Feeling a headache coming on
A pharmacist asks a customer
Telling a parent you feel unwell

faq.q: How do you say I'm sick in Korean?
faq.a: Casually, 아파. Politely, 아파요. To be specific, name the body part, like 머리 아파요 (I have a headache).

faq.q: What is the difference between apa and appa?
faq.a: 아파 (apa) means "it hurts". 아빠 (appa) means "dad". The double ㅃ makes a tense, sharper sound.

faq.q: How do you say ouch in Korean?
faq.a: People usually say 아야! or just 아! when something suddenly hurts. 아파! is also common.

intro: 더워 (deowo) means "It's hot" or "I'm hot" in casual Korean. It is used for hot weather or a hot room, not for hot food or spicy taste.
literal: It is the casual form of 덥다 (to be hot). The ㅂ in 덥다 changes to 우 when an ending is added, which gives 더워.
usage: Say 더워 on a sticky summer day, in a crowded bus, or when the heating is too high. Koreans also love the exaggeration 더워 죽겠어 (I'm dying of heat).
Korean uses different words for different kinds of hot. 더워 is for air and weather, 뜨거워 is for things that are hot to touch, like soup or coffee, and 매워 is for spicy food.
The polite form is 더워요. To ask if someone is hot, say 더워? or 더워요?

forms.note: For hot objects, food and drinks.

examples.context: Stepping outside in August
Complaining to a friend
Asking a coworker coming in from outside

faq.q: What is the difference between deowo and tteugeowo?
faq.a: 더워 is for hot weather or air. 뜨거워 is for things that are hot to touch, like a cup of tea.

faq.q: How do you say spicy in Korean?
faq.a: 매워 (maewo). 더워 is never used for spicy food.

faq.q: How do you say it's hot politely?
faq.a: Say 더워요, or 덥네요 when you are commenting on it.

intro: 추워 (chuwo) means "It's cold" or "I'm cold" in casual Korean. It is used for cold weather or a chilly room.
literal: It is the casual form of 춥다 (to be cold). The ㅂ changes to 우 when an ending is added, giving 추워.
usage: Say 추워 on a winter morning, in a freezing office, or when you're shivering. Like with heat, Koreans exaggerate: 추워 죽겠어 (I'm freezing to death).
추워 is for air and weather, and for how your body feels. For something cold to touch, like ice or a cold drink, use 차가워. 시원해 means pleasantly cool, as in a cool breeze or a refreshing drink.
The polite form is 추워요. 안 추워? (Aren't you cold?) is a caring question you will hear a lot in dramas, often right before someone offers their jacket.

forms.note: For cold objects, food and drinks.

examples.context: Opening the door on a winter morning
Telling a coworker about the weather
Checking on a friend in a thin jacket

faq.q: What is the difference between chuwo and chagawo?
faq.a: 추워 is for cold weather or feeling cold. 차가워 is for things that are cold to touch, like ice.

faq.q: How do you say it's cold politely?
faq.a: Say 추워요, or 춥네요 when you are commenting on the weather.

faq.q: What does chuwo jukgesseo mean?
faq.a: 추워 죽겠어 means "I'm freezing". Literally it is "I'm so cold I could die", a common casual exaggeration.

intro: 최애 (choeae) is Korean slang for your number one favorite, most often your favorite member of a K-pop group. It is the Korean word for what English-speaking fans call a "bias". It also works for anything you love most, like a favorite song, food or drama.
literal: 최 means "most" and 애 means "love", so it is literally "most loved". It is a short form of 최고로 애정하는 (the one I love the most).
usage: Fans ask each other 최애 누구야? ("Who's your bias?") all the time. You can also put 최애 in front of a noun: 최애 곡 (favorite song), 최애 음식 (favorite food), 최애 드라마 (favorite drama).

It is casual and playful, but it is so widespread that people of many ages use it, and you will hear it on Korean TV variety shows. With people you don't know well, 제일 좋아하는 (the one I like most) is the plain, neutral way to say it.
Your second favorite is your 차애 (chaeae). Saying someone is your 최애 is a fun way to show affection, even about a friend or a pet.

forms.note: Short for 최애 캐릭터, used for dramas, games and anime.
The member you like after your 최애.
Neutral, non-slang way to say it.

examples.context: Asking a new friend about their K-pop taste
Sharing a playlist with a friend
examples.en: This song is my favorite song

examples.context: Telling a coworker about a show you love

faq.q: What does choeae mean in K-pop?
faq.a: It means your favorite member, the same as "bias" in English fan talk. 최애 누구야? means "Who's your bias?"

faq.q: Can choeae be used for things other than idols?
faq.a: Yes. You can say 최애 음식 (favorite food), 최애 카페 (favorite cafe) or 최애 드라마 (favorite drama).

faq.q: What is the difference between choeae and chaeae?
faq.a: 최애 is your number one favorite. 차애 is your second favorite.

intro: 차애 (chaeae) is Korean fan slang for your second favorite, usually the member of a K-pop group you like right after your 최애 (choeae, top favorite). English-speaking fans often compare it to a "bias wrecker", the member who threatens to become your favorite.
literal: 차 means "next" or "second", and 애 means "love". It was made to pair with 최애 ("most loved").
usage: Fans use 차애 when talking about their ranking of members: 최애 is number one and 차애 is number two. Some joke about 차차애 for number three.
A common fan joke is that your 차애 slowly turns into your 최애. It is casual fan talk, best used with friends and other fans.

Strictly speaking, 차애 just means second favorite. The English "bias wrecker" has a slightly different feeling, a member who keeps pulling your attention away from your bias, but the two are often used as rough equivalents.

examples.context: Explaining your favorite members
examples.en: My second favorite is the youngest member

examples.context: Admitting your feelings are changing
examples.en: I think my second favorite will become my top favorite

examples.context: Chatting with another fan

faq.q: Is chaeae the same as bias wrecker?
faq.a: Close, but not exactly. 차애 simply means your second favorite, while "bias wrecker" suggests someone threatening to replace your bias. Fans often treat them as equivalents.

faq.q: How do you say third favorite in Korean?
faq.a: Some fans jokingly say 차차애 (chachaae). It is playful and less common than 최애 and 차애.

meaning: Becoming a fan / falling into it
intro: 입덕 (ipdeok) is Korean fan slang for becoming a fan of someone or something, like falling into a fandom. You might say you "ipdeok-ed" after one music video or one drama scene. The verb is 입덕하다.
literal: 입 means "to enter" and 덕 comes from 덕후 (deokhu), "devoted fan" or "geek". So 입덕 is literally "entering fandom".
usage: Fans talk about their 입덕 계기, the moment or video that got them hooked, and share 입덕 영상, videos that make new fans. It is often used for K-pop, but works for any hobby: anime, a drama, an actor, even a sport.
There is a playful phrase 입덕 부정기, the "denial phase" when you insist you are not really a fan yet. The opposite of 입덕 is 탈덕 (taldeok), quitting being a fan.
It is casual slang. Friends, fan communities and social media are the right place for it.

forms.note: A clip that turns people into fans.
When you won't admit you are a fan yet.

examples.context: Telling a friend about a new group you love
Explaining how you got into a group
examples.en: I became a fan after watching this stage

examples.context: Asking another fan in a fan chat

faq.q: What does ipdeok mean in K-pop?
faq.a: It means becoming a fan. If you say you 입덕했어 after a performance, you mean it made you a fan.

faq.q: What is the opposite of ipdeok?
faq.a: 탈덕 (taldeok), which means quitting being a fan.

faq.q: What is an ipdeok video?
faq.a: An 입덕 영상 is a clip that tends to turn people into fans, like a great live stage or a funny variety moment.

intro: 탈덕 (taldeok) is Korean fan slang for quitting being a fan, leaving a fandom you used to be part of. It is the opposite of 입덕 (ipdeok), becoming a fan. The verb is 탈덕하다.
literal: 탈 means "to escape" or "to leave", and 덕 comes from 덕후 (deokhu), "devoted fan". So 탈덕 is literally "leaving fandom".
usage: People 탈덕 for many reasons: losing interest, growing older, or being let down by a scandal. Fans also joke 탈덕은 없다 ("there is no quitting") about groups they will never stop loving.
A softer word is 휴덕, "taking a break from fandom", when you plan to come back. Someone who left and returned might say they came back after 탈덕.
It is casual slang for friends and fan communities. Be gentle with it: telling a fan that you've 탈덕 from their favorite can feel a bit hurtful.

forms.note: Taking a break, not quitting for good.

examples.context: Telling an old fan friend some news
Surprised a friend left the fandom
examples.en: Why did you quit being a fan?

examples.context: Promising loyalty in a fan chat
examples.en: I could never quit being a fan

faq.q: What does taldeok mean?
faq.a: It means leaving a fandom, no longer being a fan of someone or something.

faq.q: What is the difference between taldeok and hyudeok?
faq.a: 탈덕 means quitting. 휴덕 means taking a break from being a fan, with the idea you might come back.

intro: 덕후 (deokhu) is Korean slang for a devoted fan or geek, someone who is deeply into a hobby, like K-pop, anime, games or a particular actor. It is close to "otaku" or "nerd" in English, and these days it is usually said with pride or affection.
literal: It comes from 오덕후, a Korean adaptation of the Japanese word otaku (오타쿠). 오덕후 was later shortened to 덕후, and the piece 덕 now appears in many fan words like 입덕 and 덕질.
usage: Put a topic in front of it to say what kind of fan someone is: 애니 덕후 (anime geek), 게임 덕후 (gaming geek), 빵 덕후 (bread lover). It once sounded more negative, but now many people call themselves 덕후 happily.
Fan activities are called 덕질, and someone whose fandom paid off, like meeting their idol or working with them, is a 성덕, short for 성공한 덕후 (successful fan).
It is casual. Calling yourself a 덕후 is fine anywhere friendly, but calling a stranger one could sound like teasing.

forms.note: Collecting, streaming, going to concerts and so on.
Short for 성공한 덕후, a fan whose dream came true.

examples.context: Introducing your hobby
Talking about your sister
examples.en: My older sister is a K-pop fanatic

examples.context: Impressed by a friend's huge collection

faq.q: Is deokhu an insult?
faq.a: Not usually anymore. It once sounded negative, but now people use it proudly for themselves. Said in a mocking tone, it can still tease.

faq.q: What is the difference between deokhu and otaku?
faq.a: 덕후 comes from otaku, but in Korean it is broader and friendlier. It can mean a fan of anything, from K-pop to bread.

faq.q: What does seongdeok mean?
faq.a: 성덕 is short for 성공한 덕후, a "successful fan" who got to meet or work with the person they admire.

intro: 사생 (sasaeng) is short for 사생팬, an obsessive fan who invades a celebrity's private life, for example by following them, waiting outside their home or getting their personal phone number. It is a strongly negative word, close to "stalker fan".
literal: 사생 means "private life" (as in 사생활), and 팬 is "fan". So a 사생팬 is a fan who goes after an idol's private life.
usage: You hear 사생 in news stories and fan discussions about idols being followed to airports, dorms or hotels, or having their private flights and phone numbers leaked. Agencies and fans regularly speak out against it.
Most fans are very clear that 사생 are not real fans, and calling someone a 사생 is a serious accusation. It is never a compliment or a joke about being a big fan.
If you just mean a passionate fan, use 덕후 (deokhu) or say someone is a big fan (찐팬). Keep 사생 for behavior that crosses the line.

forms.note: Taxis hired to chase idols' cars.

examples.context: Reacting to news about an idol being followed
Correcting someone in a fan chat
Passing on news to a friend
examples.en: I heard they moved dorms because of sasaengs

faq.q: What is a sasaeng fan?
faq.a: A fan who invades a celebrity's private life by stalking them, tracking their schedule or contacting them privately. The behavior is widely condemned.

faq.q: Is sasaeng the same as a big fan?
faq.a: No. A big, devoted fan is a 덕후 or 찐팬. 사생 is only for fans who cross into stalking and harassment.

intro: 셀카 (selca) is the Korean word for a selfie, a photo you take of yourself. It is everyday Korean that everyone uses, from teens to grandparents, and K-pop fans often use "selca" in English too.
literal: It is a Korean-made blend of the English words "self" and "camera" (셀프 + 카메라). It was used in Korea before "selfie" became common in English.
usage: The common verb is 셀카 찍다, "to take a selfie". 셀카봉 is a selfie stick, and people talk about their best angle, sometimes called 얼짱 각도 (ulzzang angle).
셀카 is neutral and fine in any situation. You can ask a stranger at a fan event 같이 셀카 찍어도 돼요? ("Can I take a selfie with you?").
A photo someone else takes of you is just 사진 (photo), not 셀카.

forms.note: Hashtag-style word for posting selfies on Instagram.

examples.context: At a cafe with a friend
Texting someone you're dating
Asking a new acquaintance politely

faq.q: What does selca mean?
faq.a: It means selfie. It comes from "self" + "camera" and is written 셀카 in Korean.

faq.q: Is selca slang or normal Korean?
faq.a: It started as a coined word, but it is now ordinary Korean that people of all ages use.

faq.q: How do you say take a selfie in Korean?
faq.a: 셀카 찍다. To suggest it to a friend, say 셀카 찍자 ("Let's take a selfie").

intro: 한류 (hallyu) means the Korean Wave, the worldwide popularity of Korean pop culture such as K-dramas, K-pop, movies, food and beauty. If you are reading this because you love a Korean show or group, you are part of 한류.
literal: 한 refers to Korea and 류 means "flow" or "current", so it is "Korean current" or "Korean wave". It is pronounced 할류 (hallyu), which is why the romanization has a double L.
usage: The term spread from around the late 1990s, when Korean dramas and pop music became popular in China and other parts of Asia, and it grew worldwide over the following decades.
It is a neutral word used in news, schools and daily talk. People talk about 한류 스타 (hallyu stars), 한류 팬 (hallyu fans) and 한류 열풍 (hallyu fever).
Many learners say they started Korean thanks to 한류. In Korea, saying 한류 덕분에 한국어를 배워요 ("I'm learning Korean thanks to hallyu") is an easy conversation starter.

forms.note: A fan of Korean pop culture.
Newer term often used alongside 한류.

examples.context: Talking about Korean culture abroad
Explaining why you study Korean
examples.en: I'm learning Korean thanks to hallyu

examples.context: Introducing yourself at a language exchange

faq.q: What does hallyu mean?
faq.a: It means the Korean Wave, the global popularity of Korean dramas, music, movies, food and beauty.

faq.q: Why is it spelled hallyu and not hanryu?
faq.a: Because 한류 is pronounced 할류. The ㄴ sound changes to ㄹ before ㄹ, so it sounds like hal-lyu.

faq.q: When did hallyu start?
faq.a: The term became popular around the late 1990s, when Korean dramas and K-pop took off in China and other parts of Asia.

intro: 인싸 (insa) is Korean slang for a popular, outgoing person who is at the center of things and knows all the trends. It is short for 인사이더, the English word "insider". The opposite is 아싸 (assa), an outsider.
literal: It is a shortened form of 인사이더 (insider). The ㅆ in 인싸 makes it sound punchier and more like slang.
usage: Call someone a 인싸 if they have tons of friends, get invited everywhere and always know what's trending. It is usually a compliment, sometimes with light teasing.
인싸템 ("insider item") means a trendy item everyone wants, and 핵인싸 means a super popular person. Many people joke about trying to look like a 인싸.
It is casual slang from roughly the late 2010s. Use it with friends, not in formal situations. Don't confuse it with 인사 (insa with a softer s), which means "greeting".

examples.context: Describing a friend who knows everyone
Seeing a friend's packed weekend schedule
Joking about your new year's goal

faq.q: What does insa mean in Korean slang?
faq.a: 인싸 means a popular, social person, from the English word "insider".

faq.q: Is insa a compliment?
faq.a: Usually, yes. It means you are social and on trend. It is casual slang for friends.

faq.q: Is 인싸 the same as 인사?
faq.a: No. 인사 means "greeting", as in 인사하다 (to say hello). 인싸 has a tense ㅆ and is the slang word.

intro: 아싸 (assa) is Korean slang for an outsider, someone who doesn't really fit into the popular crowd or prefers to keep to themselves. It is short for 아웃사이더, the English word "outsider", and is the opposite of 인싸 (insa).
literal: It is a shortened form of 아웃사이더 (outsider). Be aware that 앗싸, a happy cheer like "Yay!" or "Yes!", sounds the same when spoken, so context tells you which one it is.
usage: People often call themselves 아싸 in a self-mocking way, for example at college when they eat alone or skip group events. 자발적 아싸 ("voluntary outsider") is someone who chooses to be on their own and is happy that way.
Calling someone else an 아싸 can sting, so be careful. Saying it about yourself is usually light and humorous.
If you hear 앗싸! shouted after winning a game or getting good news, it is the cheer "Yay!", not "outsider".

forms.note: A cheer that sounds the same. Different word.

examples.context: Joking about your social life
Talking about university days
examples.en: I was an outsider in college

examples.context: Explaining why you like eating alone

faq.q: What does assa mean in Korean?
faq.a: As slang, 아싸 means an outsider or loner, from the English "outsider". It is the opposite of 인싸 (insider).

faq.q: Why do Koreans shout assa when they win?
faq.a: That is 앗싸, a cheer like "Yay!" or "Yes!". It sounds the same as 아싸 (outsider) but is a different word.

faq.q: Is calling someone assa rude?
faq.a: It can be. People often use it about themselves as a joke, but calling someone else an outsider may hurt.

intro: 갑질 (gapjil) means abusing your power over people below you, like a boss humiliating staff or a customer screaming at a store worker. It is a common word in Korean news and everyday talk, and it is always a criticism.
literal: In Korean contracts, the stronger party is called 갑 and the weaker party 을. 질 is a suffix for an action, often a negative one. So 갑질 is "acting like the 갑", using your upper hand to mistreat others.
usage: You hear 갑질 about bosses, rich customers, landlords or big companies who treat workers, tenants or smaller partners badly. Several real-life cases have led to public anger and new workplace rules in Korea.
The verb is 갑질하다, and someone who does it is sometimes called a 갑질 boss or 갑질 customer, for example 손님 갑질 (customer power trips). 을 is used for the side being mistreated.
It is a strong criticism but not a swear word, so it appears in news reports and polite conversation. Accusing someone of 갑질 to their face is confrontational.

forms.en: The powerful side and the weaker side
forms.note: The contract terms behind the word.
Someone with overwhelming power in a deal.

examples.context: Pointing out unfair treatment
A cafe worker venting to a friend
examples.en: The customers' power trips are so bad

examples.context: Standing up to a rude boss

faq.q: What does gapjil mean?
faq.a: It means abusing your power over people in a weaker position, like bosses mistreating staff or customers bullying workers.

faq.q: What do gap and eul mean?
faq.a: In Korean contracts, 갑 is the stronger party and 을 the weaker one. People now use them to describe any power imbalance.

faq.q: Is gapjil a bad word?
faq.a: It is not profanity, and it appears in the news. But it is always a criticism of someone's behavior.

intro: 재벌 (chaebol) means a huge family-controlled business group in Korea, and also the very rich families who run them. In K-dramas, the "chaebol heir" (재벌 2세) is a classic character: the rich, often arrogant son or daughter of a business empire.
literal: 재 means "wealth" and 벌 means "clan" or "group", so it is roughly "wealth clan". The word entered English as "chaebol" because of how often it appears in news about the Korean economy.
usage: In news and economics, 재벌 refers to big family-run conglomerates and the debates around their power. In daily talk and dramas, it often just means "super rich", as in 재벌 2세 (second-generation chaebol heir) or 재벌 3세 (third generation).
It is a neutral word, but it can carry criticism, especially when linked to stories of 갑질 (abuse of power) or special treatment.
Joking that someone is a 재벌 means they spend like they are rich. Romance plots between a 재벌 and an ordinary person are so common that they are almost a genre.

forms.note: Second generation of a chaebol family.
More neutral word for big companies.

examples.context: Gossiping about a friend's new boyfriend
examples.en: They say that guy is a chaebol heir

examples.context: Talking about your drama taste
Teasing a friend who loves rich-guy romances
examples.en: You want to marry a chaebol?

faq.q: What does chaebol mean in K-dramas?
faq.a: It usually means a super rich family that owns a giant company. The 재벌 2세 (chaebol heir) is a common drama lead.

faq.q: Is chaebol an English word?
faq.a: Yes. English dictionaries borrowed it from Korean 재벌 to describe Korean family-run conglomerates.

faq.q: How is chaebol pronounced in Korean?
faq.a: Closer to "jae-beol". 재벌 is the Korean spelling, and "chaebol" is an older romanization.

intro: 몸짱 (momjjang) is Korean slang for a person with a great, fit body, or for having one. If someone works out a lot and looks toned, friends might call them a 몸짱. It is the body version of 얼짱 (ulzzang, "best face").
literal: 몸 means "body" and 짱 (jjang) means "the best", so it is literally "best body".
usage: People use 몸짱 as a compliment, and many set 몸짱 되기 ("becoming a momjjang") as a fitness goal, especially before summer or the new year.
It is casual and light. You might compliment a friend with 완전 몸짱이다! after their workout progress.
Comments about someone's body can be sensitive, so save it for friends who are proud of their fitness rather than strangers or coworkers.

examples.context: Proud of your gym progress
examples.en: I worked out and got really fit

examples.context: Making a new year's resolution
examples.en: This year I'm going to get really fit

examples.context: Complimenting a friend at the beach

faq.q: What does momjjang mean?
faq.a: It means someone with a great, fit body. 몸 is "body" and 짱 is "the best".

faq.q: Is momjjang a compliment?
faq.a: Yes, but it is casual and about someone's body, so use it with friends rather than strangers.

intro: 올킬 (allkill) is Korean slang, used most in K-pop, for a song reaching number one on all of Korea's major music charts at the same time. More broadly it means sweeping everything, like winning every round of a game.
literal: It comes from the English words "all kill", meaning "taking out everyone". In K-pop it means the song beat every competitor on every chart.
usage: Fans celebrate when a new song 올킬했다 ("all-killed"), meaning it hit number one on the main real-time music charts. A stricter version is the 퍼펙트 올킬 (Perfect All-Kill, often written PAK), tracked by the chart site iChart, which requires the top spot across both real-time and daily charts plus iChart's weekly chart.
Outside music, 올킬 can mean dominating anything: sweeping every game, every award or every category in a contest.
It is casual fan and internet talk, most common in fan communities, news headlines about charts and variety shows.

forms.note: The strictest chart record, tracked by iChart.
The charts fans are talking about.

examples.context: Excited fan sharing chart news
examples.en: The new song all-killed the music charts

examples.context: Checking the charts with a friend
Passing on the news in a group chat
examples.en: Whoa, they say it's a chart all-kill

faq.q: What does all-kill mean in K-pop?
faq.a: It means a song reached number one on all of Korea's major music charts at the same time.

faq.q: What is a perfect all-kill?
faq.a: A stricter record tracked by the chart site iChart: the song tops the real-time and daily charts as well as iChart's weekly chart.

faq.q: Can allkill be used outside music?
faq.a: Yes. It can mean winning or sweeping everything, like every game or award.

intro: 대상 (daesang) means the grand prize, the top award at a Korean awards show. In K-pop and K-drama fandom, winning a 대상, such as Artist of the Year at a music awards show or the top acting award at a year-end drama awards, is one of the biggest honors there is.
literal: 대 means "big" or "great" and 상 means "prize" or "award". A different word spelled the same way, 대상 (對象), means "target" or "object", as in 대상 연령 (target age), so context tells them apart.
usage: Year-end award shows hand out several prizes, but the 대상 is the last and biggest one. Fans count how many 대상 their favorite artist has won as proof of their success.
You say 대상을 받다 or 대상을 타다, "to receive the grand prize". TV networks hold their own year-end awards for dramas and entertainment shows, each with its own 대상.
The word itself is standard Korean, fine in any situation. Congratulating someone with 대상 축하해요! is natural and polite.

forms.note: A main category prize, below the 대상.

examples.context: Asking a friend after an awards show
examples.en: Who won the grand prize this year?

examples.context: Congratulating a fellow fan or the artist
Celebrating your favorite group's win
examples.en: They finally won the grand prize

faq.q: What is a daesang in K-pop?
faq.a: It is the grand prize at a music awards show, like Artist, Album or Song of the Year. It is the highest honor of the night.

faq.q: Does daesang have other meanings?
faq.a: Yes. A different 대상 means "target" or "subject", as in 대상 연령 (target age). Context makes it clear.

faq.q: How do you say win a daesang in Korean?
faq.a: 대상을 받다 or 대상을 타다.

intro: 어이없어 (eoieopseo) means "This is ridiculous!", "Unbelievable!" or "I'm speechless". Koreans say it when something is so absurd, unfair or silly that they don't know how to react. It is a casual form of the adjective 어이없다.
literal: It is literally "there is no 어이". It is close in meaning to 어처구니없다, which also means "absurd". Popular stories explain 어이 as part of a millstone, but the origin is uncertain, so it is best simply learned as "absurd".
usage: Use 어이없어 when someone does something outrageous, like cutting in line, or when news is so silly it makes you laugh in disbelief. It can be annoyed or amused, depending on tone.
It is casual, so use it with friends. With people you should be polite to, 어이없어요 is the polite form, but saying it about something they did will still sound like a complaint.
Shorter reactions with a similar feeling are 헐 (heol) and 뭐야 (mwoya). 어이없네 adds a sense of just realizing how ridiculous something is.

examples.context: Someone cuts in front of you in line
Reading a silly news headline
Telling a friend about a strange situation
examples.en: It was so absurd that I laughed

faq.q: What does eoieopseo mean?
faq.a: It means "This is ridiculous" or "Unbelievable". People say it about something absurd or unfair.

faq.q: Is eoieopseo rude?
faq.a: It is not a swear word, but it is casual and shows annoyance. Saying it to an elder about something they did would sound disrespectful.

faq.q: What is the polite form of eoieopseo?
faq.a: 어이없어요. Even so, it is a complaint, so use it carefully.

intro: 노래방 (noraebang) means a karaoke room, a place where you rent a private room by the hour to sing with friends. It is one of the most popular ways to hang out in Korea, from students to coworkers.
literal: 노래 means "song" and 방 means "room", so it is literally "song room".
usage: Unlike bar karaoke in many countries, a 노래방 gives your group its own room with a screen, microphones and often tambourines. The machine may give you a score after each song, which can get very competitive.
It is a classic 2차 (second round) after dinner or a company 회식. 코인노래방 (coin karaoke) offers tiny booths where you pay per song, popular for singing alone or in pairs.
The word is standard Korean and fine anywhere. 노래방 가자! is an easy way to invite friends.

forms.note: The next stop after dinner, often 노래방.

examples.context: Inviting friends after dinner
Choosing songs with a friend
examples.en: What should we sing at karaoke?

examples.context: Suggesting the next stop to coworkers
examples.en: How about karaoke for round two?

faq.q: What is a noraebang?
faq.a: A Korean karaoke room. You rent a private room with friends and pay by the hour, or per song at coin karaoke.

faq.q: Is noraebang the same as karaoke?
faq.a: Basically yes, but a 노래방 gives each group its own private room instead of singing in front of a whole bar.

faq.q: What is a coin noraebang?
faq.a: A 코인노래방 has small booths where you pay per song, great for singing alone or with one friend.

intro: 피시방 (pc bang) means a PC room, a gaming cafe where you pay by the hour to play computer games on powerful PCs. The sign usually reads PC방, and it is a big part of Korean gaming and youth culture.
literal: 피시 is the Korean spelling of "PC" and 방 means "room". The word is most often written PC방, with English letters.
usage: PC방 are found all over Korea, many open 24 hours, with fast computers, comfortable chairs and popular games ready to play. Friends go together to play team games side by side.
You can usually order food and drinks right from your seat, and instant ramen at a PC방 is famous among gamers. Short slang for it is 피방.
The word is neutral and used by everyone. Saying 피시방 갈래? is an easy way to ask a friend to go game.

forms.note: The usual written form on signs.

forms.en: To go to a PC room

examples.context: Asking a friend after school
examples.en: Want to go to the PC room?

examples.context: Explaining why you're tired
examples.en: I gamed all night at the PC room

examples.context: Recommending the food to a visitor
examples.en: PC room ramen is the tastiest

faq.q: What is a PC bang?
faq.a: A Korean gaming cafe where you pay by the hour to use high-end computers. The sign usually says PC방.

faq.q: How do you write PC bang in Korean?
faq.a: Most signs write PC방. Spelled fully in Korean letters, it is 피시방.

faq.q: Can you eat at a PC bang?
faq.a: Yes. Most let you order snacks, drinks and meals like ramen from your seat.

intro: 찜질방 (jjimjilbang) means a Korean public spa or bathhouse with hot saunas, baths and big shared rest areas. People go to relax, sweat, eat snacks, nap and spend time with family or friends, sometimes for hours.
literal: 찜질 means warming the body with heat, like a hot compress or a sauna, and 방 means "room". So it is roughly "heat therapy room".
usage: Visitors get a simple uniform to wear in the shared areas, which have heated rooms at different temperatures, a place to lie on the floor and a snack bar. The bathing areas are separated by gender, and you bathe without clothes there.
Classic 찜질방 snacks are baked eggs and 식혜, a sweet rice drink. People often fold a towel into a "sheep head" (양머리) shape, a look made famous by dramas and variety shows.
Many are open late or around the clock, and some travelers even stay the night. The word is standard Korean and fine to use anywhere.

forms.note: Simpler bathhouse without the big shared lounge.

examples.context: Suggesting a relaxing weekend
examples.en: Let's go to a jjimjilbang and rest

examples.context: Telling a friend about your day
examples.en: I ate eggs at the jjimjilbang

examples.context: Enjoying a cold drink after the sauna

faq.q: What is a jjimjilbang?
faq.a: A Korean public spa with saunas, baths and shared rest areas where people relax, eat snacks and nap.

faq.q: Do you wear clothes in a jjimjilbang?
faq.a: In the shared areas you wear the uniform they give you. In the gender-separated baths, people bathe without clothes.

faq.q: Can you sleep at a jjimjilbang?
faq.a: Many are open late or 24 hours, and some people stay overnight, though rules differ by place.

intro: 교포 (gyopo) means an ethnic Korean who lives abroad, especially someone born or raised overseas, like a Korean American or Korean Canadian. In Korea it is often used for people who look Korean but grew up speaking another language.
literal: 교 means "living away from home" and 포 comes from 동포, "fellow countrymen". You can add a place: 재미교포 is a Korean living in America, 재일교포 a Korean living in Japan.
usage: 교포 is a common, mostly neutral word, and many overseas Koreans call themselves 교포. You also hear 교포 발음 (gyopo accent) for the way some overseas Koreans speak Korean.
The word can sometimes make people feel like outsiders, since it marks them as not fully "from Korea". Official language often uses 재외동포 (overseas Koreans) instead.

Different communities have different histories. For example, 재일교포 refers to Koreans in Japan, many descended from people who moved there during the colonial period, so it is worth learning each group's story.

examples.context: Introducing yourself in Korea
Explaining a friend's fluent English
examples.en: They grew up abroad, so their English is good

examples.context: Chatting at a language exchange

faq.q: What does gyopo mean?
faq.a: It means an ethnic Korean living abroad, especially someone raised overseas, like a Korean American.

faq.q: Is gyopo offensive?
faq.a: Not usually. Many overseas Koreans use it for themselves. Some feel it marks them as outsiders, so the official term is 재외동포.

faq.q: What does jaemi gyopo mean?
faq.a: 재미교포 means a Korean living in America, or a Korean American.

intro: 한 (han) means a deep, lingering feeling of sorrow, regret and resentment that builds up from suffering or injustice that was never resolved. It is often described as a key emotion in Korean culture, and it is a common theme in Korean dramas, films, literature and traditional songs.
literal: This 한 is written 恨 in Chinese characters, meaning "resentment" or "regret". The same sound 한 has other meanings too, such as "one" (as in 한 번, once) and "Korea" (as in 한국), so context matters.
usage: People say 한이 맺히다, "han is knotted up", for grief or bitterness that settles deep in the heart, and 한을 풀다, "to release han", when that pain is finally eased, for example when a long-hoped-for wish comes true or justice is done.

Writers often link 한 to Korea's history of hardship, and it is sometimes called uniquely Korean. Some scholars caution against that idea, since similar feelings exist everywhere, so it is fair to call 한 a deeply Korean concept without claiming no one else feels it.

한 is a serious, heavy word. It is used about real, long-held pain, not everyday annoyance. It is often discussed alongside 정 (jeong), the warm bond between people, as two emotions central to Korean culture.

forms.note: Grief or resentment that settles deep inside.
To finally ease a long-held pain or wish.
Venting or making up for long-held pain.

examples.context: A grandmother talking about her hard life
examples.en: Han has built up in me

examples.context: After finally achieving a lifelong dream
Describing a character in a novel
examples.en: Han still remains in his heart

faq.q: What is han in Korean culture?
faq.a: 한 is a deep, lingering sorrow and resentment from pain or injustice that was never resolved. It is a major theme in Korean art and storytelling.

faq.q: Is han unique to Korea?
faq.a: It is often described that way, and the concept is strongly tied to Korean culture. Many scholars note that similar feelings exist elsewhere, so it is best seen as a Korean way of naming a human experience.

faq.q: Does han mean one in Korean?
faq.a: Yes, a different 한 means "one", as in 한 번 (once). It also means "Korea" in words like 한국. The emotion 한 is a separate word.

intro: 소주 (soju) is Korea's most popular alcoholic drink, a clear liquor usually sold in small green bottles. It is cheap, fairly strong and served in tiny shot glasses with meals, especially grilled meat.
literal: The word comes from Chinese characters meaning "burned liquor", a reference to how it was originally made by distilling.
usage: Soju is drunk with food, not on its own, and it is shared. Friends pour for each other rather than for themselves, so keep an eye on your neighbor's glass and refill it when it is empty.

With someone older or senior, hold the bottle with two hands (or one hand supporting the other arm) when you pour, receive their pour with your glass in two hands, and turn your head slightly away when you drink. Among close friends of the same age, these rules relax.
The word itself is neutral and fine with anyone. Saying 소주 한잔해요 ("Let's have a drink of soju") is a common, friendly way to invite someone out after work.

forms.note: Often means "a drink" in general, as in 소주 한잔하자 ("Let's grab a drink").
How you order it at a restaurant.
Short for 소주 + 맥주 (beer). A very popular mix.
The small shot glass soju is served in.

examples.context: Ordering at a barbecue restaurant
Texting a friend in the evening
examples.en: Want to grab some soju tonight?

examples.context: Trying soju for the first time

faq.q: How strong is soju?
faq.a: Most green-bottle soju today is around 16 to 17 percent alcohol, roughly between wine and vodka. Traditional soju can be much stronger.

faq.q: How do you drink soju politely?
faq.a: Pour for others instead of yourself, use two hands when pouring for or receiving from someone older, and turn your head a little away from them when you drink.

faq.q: What does soju taste like?
faq.a: Plain soju tastes clean and slightly sweet with a sharp alcohol bite. Many Koreans describe it as 쓰다 (bitter). Flavored versions are fruitier.

intro: 막걸리 (makgeolli) is a traditional Korean rice wine. It is milky white, a little sweet and a little fizzy, and usually milder than soju.
literal: The name is usually explained as 막 ("roughly" or "just now") plus 거르다 ("to strain"), describing a drink that is roughly strained, which is why it looks cloudy.
usage: Makgeolli is often poured into small metal or ceramic bowls instead of glasses. Gently turn or tip the bottle before opening, because the rice settles at the bottom.
Many Koreans pair it with 파전 (pajeon, savory green onion pancake), especially on rainy days. It is also a classic drink after hiking or at a casual country-style restaurant.
The same drinking manners as soju apply: pour for others, and use two hands with someone older.

forms.note: The classic pairing people mention together.
A similar rice wine with grains of rice floating on top.

examples.context: Looking out at the rain
Asking a visitor about Korean drinks
Ordering with friends

faq.q: Is makgeolli the same as soju?
faq.a: No. Soju is clear and distilled, while makgeolli is cloudy, fermented rice wine with lower alcohol, usually around 6 percent.

faq.q: Why do people drink makgeolli on rainy days?
faq.a: It is a popular custom to have makgeolli with pajeon when it rains. People often say the sound of rain is like the sizzle of pancakes frying.

faq.q: Should you shake makgeolli?
faq.a: Mix it gently by turning the bottle upside down a few times. Shaking it hard can make the fizzy drink spill when you open it.

intro: 안주 (anju) means food that you eat while drinking alcohol. It can be anything from dried squid and nuts to fried chicken or a big stew shared at the table.
literal: It is an old Sino-Korean word. In everyday Korean it simply means food that goes with alcohol, and 술안주 says the same thing even more clearly.
