usage: In Korea, drinking usually comes with food. Many bars expect each table to order at least one anju dish, and friends often choose a place based on its anju.
Popular anju include fried chicken, 파전 (green onion pancake), 오뎅탕 (fish cake soup), 골뱅이 (spicy sea snails) and simple dried snacks called 마른안주.
The word is neutral and fine to use with anyone, from friends to coworkers.

forms.note: 술 means alcohol. Same meaning, very common.
Dried squid, nuts, crackers and similar.

forms.en: To eat the snacks more than drink
forms.note: Playful phrase for someone who keeps eating the anju.

examples.context: Friends at a bar looking at the menu
examples.en: What should we order to eat with our drinks?

examples.context: Recommending a bar to a coworker
examples.en: The food here is really good.

examples.context: Tasting a spicy stew

faq.q: Do you have to order anju in Korea?
faq.a: At many Korean bars and pubs, yes. Each table is usually expected to order at least one food dish along with the drinks.

faq.q: What is the difference between anju and banchan?
faq.a: Anju is food eaten with alcohol. 반찬 (banchan) are side dishes eaten with rice at a meal.

faq.q: What is the most popular anju?
faq.a: Fried chicken with beer is a favorite, while pork belly, pancakes and spicy stews are common with soju.

intro: 건배 (geonbae) means "Cheers!" in Korean. People say it while raising and clinking their glasses before a drink.
literal: It comes from Chinese characters meaning "dry the cup". It is the same word as Chinese ganbei and Japanese kanpai.
usage: Say 건배! together as glasses touch. At a group dinner, one person often leads with a short toast called 건배사, and everyone shouts back. A common call and response is "위하여!" ("To...!").
When toasting with someone older or senior, hold your glass a little lower than theirs as it clinks, and use two hands. This small gesture shows respect.
건배 is fine in any setting, from a family dinner to a company party. It does not mean you must finish your drink; that is 원샷.

forms.note: Verb form, as in 건배할까요? ("Shall we toast?").
The short speech before everyone says cheers.

examples.context: Raising glasses with friends
Suggesting a toast at dinner
Toasting a close friend

faq.q: How do you say cheers in Korean?
faq.a: Say 건배 (geonbae). In a group, people sometimes also shout 위하여 ("To...!") after a short toast.

faq.q: Is gunbae the same as geonbae?
faq.a: Yes. Gunbae is just another way of spelling 건배 in English letters.

faq.q: Is there etiquette for clinking glasses in Korea?
faq.a: With someone older or senior, hold your glass slightly lower than theirs when you clink, and hold it with two hands.

meaning: Bottoms up! / Down it in one
intro: 원샷 (wonsyat) means "Bottoms up!", drinking your whole glass in one go. It comes from the English words "one shot", said with a Korean accent.
literal: It is Konglish, a Korean word made from English. The English phrase "one shot" was borrowed and given the meaning of downing a drink in one gulp.
usage: People shout 원샷! at parties and drinking nights to encourage everyone to empty their glasses at the same time. It can be cheerful, but it can also put pressure on people.
Today, forcing someone to drink is widely seen as bad manners, and many people simply say they will sip. It is fine to reply 저는 천천히 마실게요 ("I'll drink slowly").
It is casual, but you will hear it at company dinners too. It can also be used for non-alcoholic drinks, like finishing a smoothie in one go.

forms.en: To down a drink in one go

examples.context: At a party, everyone raising glasses
Reassuring a new coworker
examples.en: You don't have to down it.

examples.context: Shocked at a friend
examples.en: You drank that in one go?

faq.q: Is wonsyat Korean or English?
faq.a: It comes from the English "one shot", but it is used as a Korean word. English speakers say "bottoms up" or "chug" instead.

faq.q: Do I have to wonsyat if someone says it?
faq.a: No. You can sip or say 저는 천천히 마실게요 ("I'll drink slowly"). Pressuring people to drink is increasingly frowned upon.

faq.q: How do you spell one shot in Korean?
faq.a: It is written 원샷. The romanization wonsyat follows the official system, but most people search for "one shot".

intro: 포장마차 (pojangmacha) is a street tent bar or food stall, usually with an orange or red plastic cover, that sells cheap drinks and snacks at night. People often shorten it to 포차 (pocha).
literal: It is made of 포장 ("covering, canvas") and 마차 ("cart, wagon"), so it literally means a covered cart.
usage: Pojangmacha are known for soju, 떡볶이, 오뎅 (fish cake skewers), 우동 and other simple food served on plastic stools. They feel informal, a little old-fashioned and very friendly.
In K-dramas, the tent bar is a classic place for heart-to-heart talks, heartbreak and late-night confessions over soju, so the word carries an emotional, nostalgic feeling.
Street tents are less common than they used to be, but many indoor bars use the name 포차 or 실내포차 ("indoor pocha") to copy the same casual mood.

forms.note: A bar inside a building with the tent-bar feeling.

forms.en: To have a drink at a tent bar
forms.note: A typical phrase for a night out.

examples.context: Inviting a friend after a long day
examples.en: Want to grab a drink at a pojangmacha?

examples.context: Talking about favorite street food
examples.en: Street tent tteokbokki is the best.

examples.context: Walking past a tent at night

faq.q: What is a pocha?
faq.a: 포차 (pocha) is the short form of 포장마차, a casual tent bar or a bar designed to feel like one.

faq.q: What do you eat at a pojangmacha?
faq.a: Simple, cheap food that goes with drinks, such as tteokbokki, fish cake skewers, noodles and stir-fried dishes.

faq.q: Why are pojangmacha in so many K-dramas?
faq.a: They are cozy, cheap and open late, so they are a natural setting for characters to drink soju and talk about their feelings.

intro: 회식 (hoesik) means a company or team dinner, usually after work and usually with drinks. It is a big part of Korean office culture.
literal: It is a Sino-Korean word made of 회 ("gather") and 식 ("eat"), so it means eating together as a group.
usage: A 회식 is usually a team meal paid for by the company or the boss. It often starts at a barbecue restaurant with soju and can move on to a second round (2차, icha) at a bar or a noraebang.

In the past it was hard to say no to 회식, and long nights of drinking were common. Many younger workers now push back, and many companies keep it shorter, make drinking optional or hold a lunch 회식 instead.
The word itself is neutral. You will hear it often in office dramas, usually with someone groaning that there is a 회식 tonight.

forms.note: Moving on to another place after the first round of the night.
Money the company sets aside for it.

examples.context: Telling your family you will be late
examples.en: We have a team dinner tonight.

examples.context: Quietly asking a coworker
examples.en: Can I skip the team dinner?

examples.context: A coworker making plans
examples.en: After the team dinner, let's go to karaoke.

faq.q: Is hoesik mandatory?
faq.a: Officially it usually is not, but in many workplaces skipping it often used to be seen as poor teamwork. Attitudes are changing, and it is becoming easier to leave early or not drink.

faq.q: Who pays for hoesik?
faq.a: Usually the company or the most senior person pays. Junior staff are rarely expected to pay.

faq.q: What is 2cha after hoesik?
faq.a: 2차 (icha) means the second round, when the group moves from the restaurant to another place such as a bar or a noraebang.

intro: 반찬 (banchan) means the side dishes served with rice in a Korean meal. Kimchi, seasoned vegetables, small fish and rolled omelet are all 반찬.
literal: It is the everyday word for any dish eaten alongside rice, from a single plate of kimchi at home to a dozen small bowls at a restaurant.
usage: At Korean restaurants, banchan are usually brought out free with the main dish, and refills are often free too. It is normal to ask politely for more.
Banchan are placed in the middle of the table and shared. Everyone takes small bites from the common plates instead of moving food onto their own.
At home, families keep 밑반찬, long-lasting side dishes stored in the fridge, so a meal can be put together quickly with rice and soup.

forms.note: Long-lasting dishes kept in the fridge at home.
A shop that sells ready-made banchan.

examples.context: Asking for a refill at a restaurant
examples.en: Could we get more side dishes, please?

examples.context: Visiting your parents
examples.en: Mom's side dishes are the best.

examples.context: Seeing the table filled with plates
examples.en: There are so many side dishes.

faq.q: Are banchan free in Korea?
faq.a: At most Korean restaurants, yes. Side dishes come free with your meal, and refills are usually free too.

faq.q: Can you ask for more banchan?
faq.a: Yes. Say 반찬 좀 더 주세요. Some restaurants have a self-serve banchan bar instead.

faq.q: Is kimchi a banchan?
faq.a: Yes. Kimchi is the most common banchan of all.

intro: 야식 (yasik) means a late-night snack or meal, food you eat late in the evening after dinner. Fried chicken, ramyeon and pig's trotters (족발) are popular choices.
literal: It is a Sino-Korean word: 야 means "night" and 식 means "food" or "eating".
usage: Ordering 야식 for delivery is a big part of Korean life, since many restaurants deliver late. Friends or roommates often ask each other 야식 먹을래? ("Want a late-night snack?").
People also joke about 야식 when dieting, because eating late is seen as the enemy of weight loss.
The word is neutral and fine with anyone.

forms.note: What to eat for a late snack.

examples.context: Roommates watching TV late
examples.en: Should we order a late-night snack?

examples.context: Talking about a diet
examples.en: I need to stop eating late at night.

examples.context: Telling a coworker about last night
examples.en: I had ramyeon as a late-night snack.

faq.q: What do Koreans eat for yasik?
faq.a: Common choices are fried chicken, ramyeon, 족발 (braised pig's trotters), 떡볶이 and pizza, often ordered for delivery.

faq.q: Is yasik the same as a midnight snack?
faq.a: Yes, very close. It can be a small snack or a full meal, as long as it is eaten late at night.

intro: 혼밥 (honbap) means eating a meal by yourself. It is a newer, casual word that became popular as more people in Korea live and eat alone.
literal: It is short for 혼자 ("alone") + 밥 ("rice, meal").
usage: Korean meals are traditionally shared, and eating alone in a restaurant used to feel awkward. Today 혼밥 is common, and many places have counter seats or single portions for solo diners.
People use it in a light, neutral way: 혼밥해요 simply means "I'm eating alone". It can sound a little lonely or a little proud, depending on tone.
It is informal, but widely understood and used in news and on menus.

forms.note: Made the same way from 혼자 + 술.
족 means a group or "tribe" of people.

examples.context: Answering a friend who asks about lunch
Recommending a restaurant
examples.en: This place is good for eating alone.

examples.context: Asking a friend

faq.q: Is honbap sad?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Many people enjoy eating alone, and the word is used in a neutral or even positive way.

faq.q: What is the difference between honbap and honsul?
faq.a: 혼밥 is eating a meal alone. 혼술 is drinking alcohol alone.

intro: 혼술 (honsul) means drinking alcohol by yourself, at home or at a bar. It is a newer, casual word that became common alongside 혼밥 (eating alone).
literal: It is short for 혼자 ("alone") + 술 ("alcohol").
usage: In Korea, drinking is traditionally a group activity with lots of pouring for each other. 혼술 describes the opposite: a quiet drink on your own, often a can of beer from the convenience store after work.
The word sounds relaxed and modern rather than worrying. Many bars now welcome solo drinkers.
It is casual but widely understood.

forms.note: The word it is modeled on.

examples.context: Texting a friend on a Friday night
Getting to know someone
Telling a friend about your evening
examples.en: I had a solo drink with convenience store beer.

faq.q: Is honsul a bad thing in Korea?
faq.a: No. It is a neutral, everyday word for having a drink on your own, often to relax after work.

faq.q: How do you say drinking alone in Korean?
faq.a: 혼술 (honsul) is the casual way. A longer way is 혼자 술 마시다.

intro: 라면 (ramyeon) means instant noodles, the packaged kind you cook in a few minutes, usually with a spicy soup. Korean ramyeon is a staple snack and quick meal.
literal: The word was borrowed from Japanese ramen, but in Korea it almost always means instant noodles rather than fresh restaurant noodles.
usage: Koreans usually say 라면을 끓이다 ("to boil ramyeon") for making it. Adding an egg, green onion or cheese is common, and eating it straight from the pot lid is a familiar habit.
The line 라면 먹고 갈래? ("Want to have some ramyeon before you go?") is well known in Korean pop culture as a flirty way to invite someone in at the end of a date, so use it with care.
The word is neutral and fine with anyone. 컵라면 is cup noodles from the convenience store.

forms.note: The kind you add hot water to.

forms.en: Want some ramyeon before you go?
forms.note: Famous flirty invitation. Can be taken romantically.

examples.context: Offering to cook for a friend
examples.en: Want me to make you some ramyeon?

examples.context: At a convenience store
At the end of an evening, with a smile
examples.en: Want to have some ramyeon before you go?

faq.q: Is ramyeon the same as ramen?
faq.a: They are related, but Korean 라면 usually means instant noodles, often spicy, while Japanese ramen is usually a fresh noodle dish from a restaurant.

faq.q: What does "ramyeon meokgo gallae" mean?
faq.a: 라면 먹고 갈래? means "Want to have some ramyeon before you go?" It is a well-known flirty line suggesting someone come inside at the end of a date.

faq.q: How do you spell ramyun in Korean?
faq.a: It is written 라면. Ramyun, ramyeon and ramyon are all spellings of the same word.

intro: 떡볶이 (tteokbokki) is a Korean dish of chewy rice cakes cooked in a sweet and spicy red sauce made with gochujang. It is one of Korea's best-loved street foods.
literal: It comes from 떡 ("rice cake") and 볶이, from 볶다 ("to stir-fry").
usage: You find tteokbokki at street stalls, snack shops called 분식집 and delivery apps. It is often eaten with 튀김 (fried snacks), 순대 (Korean blood sausage) and 오뎅 (fish cakes).
For many Koreans it is a nostalgic after-school snack. There are many versions, including soupy, cheese-topped and creamy 로제 (rosé) tteokbokki.
The word is neutral and fine with anyone. It is usually quite spicy, so 덜 맵게 해 주세요 ("Please make it less spicy") is a useful phrase.

forms.note: The category of cheap snacks tteokbokki belongs to.

examples.context: Inviting a friend after school
Taking a first bite
Ordering at a snack shop

faq.q: How do you pronounce tteokbokki?
faq.a: It sounds roughly like "tteok-bo-kki", with a tense, unaspirated "tt" and "kk". Topokki and ddeokbokki are other common spellings.

faq.q: Is tteokbokki very spicy?
faq.a: Classic tteokbokki is fairly spicy and a little sweet. Rosé and cheese versions are milder.

faq.q: What is tteok?
faq.a: 떡 is the general word for Korean rice cakes. The ones in tteokbokki are long, chewy cylinders.

intro: 삼겹살 (samgyeopsal) means pork belly, especially thick slices grilled at the table at a Korean barbecue restaurant. It is one of the most popular meals in Korea, usually eaten with soju.
literal: It is made of 삼 ("three"), 겹 ("layer") and 살 ("flesh, meat"), meaning "three-layer meat", after the stripes of fat and lean meat.
usage: The meat is grilled at the table, cut with scissors, and wrapped in lettuce or perilla leaves with garlic, ssamjang sauce and kimchi. This wrap is called 쌈 (ssam).
Usually one person takes charge of the grill. Often the youngest or most junior person offers, though many friends and bosses happily do it themselves.
March 3 is jokingly called Samgyeopsal Day, because "three" is 삼 in Korean, and some shops run deals on that day.

forms.en: To grill and eat pork belly

forms.note: Pork belly with the skin left on.
The way samgyeopsal is usually eaten.

examples.context: Planning dinner with a friend
examples.en: How about pork belly and soju?

examples.context: Ordering at a barbecue restaurant
examples.en: Two servings of pork belly, please.

examples.context: Offering to cook for the table

faq.q: What does samgyeopsal mean in English?
faq.a: It means pork belly, literally "three-layer meat", and usually refers to Korean-style grilled pork belly.

faq.q: Is it samgyupsal or samgyeopsal?
faq.a: Both are spellings of 삼겹살. Samgyeopsal follows the official romanization, and samgyupsal is a popular older spelling.

faq.q: How do you eat samgyeopsal?
faq.a: Grill it, dip it in sesame oil with salt or in ssamjang, and wrap it in lettuce with garlic and kimchi.

intro: 김밥 (gimbap) is a Korean dish of rice and fillings rolled in dried seaweed and sliced into bite-size rounds. It is cheap, easy to carry and loved as a picnic and on-the-go food.
literal: It is made of 김 ("dried seaweed sheets") and 밥 ("cooked rice").
usage: Gimbap looks a bit like sushi rolls, but the rice is usually seasoned with sesame oil and salt rather than vinegar, and fillings are typically cooked, such as egg, pickled radish, spinach, carrot, ham or tuna.
Many Koreans remember parents making gimbap for school picnics (소풍). You can buy it cheaply at snack shops and convenience stores.
It is counted in rolls with 줄, so one roll is 김밥 한 줄. 김밥을 싸다 means "to make (roll) gimbap".

forms.note: 줄 is the counter for rolls.

examples.context: Ordering at a snack shop
Telling a friend about lunch
Planning a picnic
examples.en: Let's eat gimbap at the picnic.

faq.q: Is it kimbap or gimbap?
faq.a: Both are correct spellings of 김밥. Gimbap follows the official romanization, and kimbap is the older, very common spelling.

faq.q: Is gimbap the same as sushi?
faq.a: No. They look similar, but gimbap rice is seasoned with sesame oil instead of vinegar, and the fillings are usually cooked rather than raw fish.

intro: 비빔밥 (bibimbap) is a Korean dish of rice topped with seasoned vegetables, often meat and a fried egg, and spicy gochujang sauce, all mixed together before eating.
literal: It comes from 비빔, from 비비다 ("to mix"), and 밥 ("rice"), so it literally means "mixed rice".
usage: The key step is mixing: stir everything together with your spoon until the sauce coats the rice. Koreans usually eat it with a spoon rather than chopsticks.
돌솥비빔밥 is served in a hot stone bowl, so the rice at the bottom turns crispy. The city of Jeonju is especially famous for bibimbap.
At home, people often make a quick bibimbap by mixing leftover banchan with rice, gochujang and sesame oil.

forms.note: Served in a hot stone bowl.

examples.context: Ordering for two at a restaurant
Showing a visitor how to eat it
examples.en: You have to mix bibimbap well.

examples.context: Telling a friend what you ate

faq.q: What does bibimbap mean?
faq.a: It means "mixed rice". 비빔 comes from 비비다 (to mix) and 밥 means rice.

faq.q: Do you have to mix bibimbap?
faq.a: Yes, that is the point of the dish. Mix it well so every bite has rice, vegetables and sauce.

faq.q: Is bibimbap spicy?
faq.a: It depends on how much gochujang you add. You can ask for the sauce on the side and add a little at a time.

intro: 매워 (maewo) means "It's spicy!" in casual Korean. You say it when food burns your mouth with chili heat.
literal: It is the casual present form of 맵다 ("to be spicy"). When an ending is added, the ㅂ in 맵다 changes to 우, so 맵 + 어 becomes 매워.
usage: 매워 is casual, for friends, family and people younger than you. With strangers, staff or elders, say 매워요. Both can be a statement ("It's spicy") or a question ("Is it spicy?") depending on your tone.
Korean food can be very spicy, so it helps to know 안 매워요? ("Is it not spicy?") and 덜 맵게 해 주세요 ("Please make it less spicy").
A playful slang word for someone who cannot handle spicy food is 맵찔이.

forms.note: Use with people you are not close to.

examples.context: Eating tteokbokki with a friend
Asking a server before ordering
Reassuring a friend about a dish

faq.q: How do you say spicy in Korean?
faq.a: The dictionary word is 맵다. In conversation, say 매워 casually or 매워요 politely.

faq.q: How do I ask for less spicy food in Korean?
faq.a: Say 덜 맵게 해 주세요 ("Please make it less spicy"). For no chili at all, try 안 맵게 해 주세요.

faq.q: What is the difference between maewo and maewoyo?
faq.a: 매워 is casual and 매워요 is polite. The meaning is the same.

intro: 배불러 (baebulleo) means "I'm full" in casual Korean. You say it when you have eaten so much that you cannot eat any more.
literal: It comes from 배 ("stomach") and 부르다 ("to be full"), so it literally means "my stomach is full". This 부르다 is different from the 부르다 that means "to call" or "to sing".
usage: 배불러 is casual, for friends, family and younger people. With elders or people you have just met, say 배불러요, or 배불러요, 잘 먹었습니다 to thank the cook or host.
It is the opposite of 배고파 ("I'm hungry"). To exaggerate, people say 배 터질 것 같아 ("I feel like I'm going to burst").
In Korea, hosts often keep offering food. Saying 배불러요 with a smile is a polite way to decline more.

forms.note: Use with people you are not close to.

examples.context: Leaning back after a big meal
Turning down dessert with a friend
examples.en: I'm so full I can't eat any more.

examples.context: Surprised at a friend's small appetite

faq.q: How do you say I'm full in Korean?
faq.a: Say 배불러 to friends or 배불러요 politely. Both mean "I'm full".

faq.q: What is the opposite of baebulleo?
faq.a: 배고파 (baegopa), which means "I'm hungry".

faq.q: How do I politely refuse more food in Korean?
faq.a: Smile and say 배불러요, 잘 먹었습니다 ("I'm full, thank you for the meal").

intro: ㅋㅋㅋ (kekeke) is the Korean way of typing laughter, like "LOL" or "hahaha" in English. You will see it in almost every casual Korean text chat and comment section.
literal: ㅋ is the Korean consonant for a "k" sound. Typing it again and again imitates a laughing sound like 크크크 or 킥킥, without bothering to add the vowels.
usage: The number of ㅋ changes the feeling. A single ㅋ can look dry or even sarcastic, ㅋㅋ is a light chuckle, ㅋㅋㅋ is a normal laugh, and a long row like ㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋ means you are really cracking up.

ㅋㅋㅋ feels more playful and "laughing out loud" than ㅎㅎ, which is a softer, gentler smile. Between friends, ㅋㅋㅋ is the default. With a boss, a teacher or someone older you do not know well, ㅎㅎ is the safer choice, or no laugh at all.
People often put ㅋㅋㅋ at the start or end of a message, or send it alone as a whole reply. Out loud, nobody says "kekeke"; you just laugh.

forms.note: A long row means it is really funny.
A single one can sound dry or sarcastic.
Softer, gentler laugh. Safer with people you are not close to.

examples.context: Reacting to a funny video a friend sent
Your friend tells you an outrageous plan
Agreeing with a friend's joke about yourself

faq.q: What does kkk mean in Korean texting?
faq.a: ㅋㅋㅋ, often written "kkk" in English letters, is laughter, like "LOL" or "haha". It has nothing to do with the English meaning of "KKK".

faq.q: What is the difference between ㅋㅋ and ㅎㅎ?
faq.a: ㅋㅋ is a more open, playful laugh. ㅎㅎ is a softer smile and feels a bit more polite, so it is often used with coworkers or people you just met.

faq.q: Is a single ㅋ rude?
faq.a: It can be. One ㅋ often reads as a dry, unimpressed "heh", so if something is actually funny, use at least ㅋㅋ.

intro: ㅎㅎ (hehe) is a soft laugh or smile in Korean texting, close to "hehe" or a smiley face :). It makes a message feel warm and friendly rather than serious.
literal: ㅎ is the Korean consonant for an "h" sound. Repeating it imitates gentle laughs like 하하, 히히 or 흐흐.
usage: ㅎㅎ is softer and calmer than ㅋㅋㅋ. Where ㅋㅋㅋ is laughing out loud, ㅎㅎ is more of a smile. That is why many people add it to polite messages, like 감사합니다 ㅎㅎ, to sound friendly instead of stiff.

It is one of the few texting laughs that is generally fine with coworkers, a friend's parents or someone older you text regularly. In very formal messages, such as to a professor or a client you have never met, it is still better to leave it out.
Length matters here too. A single ㅎ can feel cold or forced. ㅎㅎ is the usual, friendly amount, and a long ㅎㅎㅎㅎㅎ can come across as a shy or slightly awkward laugh.

forms.note: A single one can feel cold or forced.
Louder, more playful laugh for friends.

examples.context: Thanking a friend for a small gift
Replying to a coworker's request
Ending a text with someone you are meeting

faq.q: Can I use ㅎㅎ with my boss or someone older?
faq.a: Usually yes, if you already text with them regularly. It softens a polite message. For a very formal first contact, leave it out.

faq.q: Why do Koreans put ㅎㅎ at the end of messages?
faq.a: Plain Korean text can look blunt or cold. Adding ㅎㅎ shows you are smiling and keeps the tone friendly.

faq.q: Is ㅎㅎ the same as ㅋㅋ?
faq.a: Both are laughs, but ㅎㅎ is gentler and more like a smile, while ㅋㅋ is a bigger, more casual laugh.

intro: ㅠㅠ (yuyu) is a crying face in Korean texting, used to show you are sad, disappointed, touched or whining a little. It works much like 😭 or T_T.
literal: ㅠ is the Korean vowel "yu". Its two short strokes hanging down look like tears falling from two closed eyes, so ㅠㅠ is a little face crying.
usage: People use ㅠㅠ for big and small feelings: a failed test, a canceled plan, missing someone, or being so moved by a kind message that you could cry. It can also be a cute, whiny way to ask for something.
More ㅠ means more emotion. ㅠㅠ is the usual amount, while ㅠㅠㅠㅠㅠ is dramatic sobbing. ㅜㅜ is the same face with slightly different tears and is used the same way.
It is casual but not rude, so friends, family and close coworkers all see it often. In a polite message like 죄송해요 ㅠㅠ it can make an apology sound sincere and soft, but skip it in formal emails.

forms.note: A long row is very dramatic.
A cute version with a little mouth.

examples.context: Texting someone you have not seen in a while
Telling a friend about your exam
Replying to a sweet birthday message

faq.q: Why is ㅠㅠ a crying face?
faq.a: The vowel ㅠ has two lines hanging down. Side by side, they look like two eyes with tears running down.

faq.q: What is the difference between ㅠㅠ and ㅜㅜ?
faq.a: There is no real difference in meaning. Both are crying faces; some people just prefer the look of one or the other.

faq.q: Is ㅠㅠ always sad?
faq.a: No. It is also used when you are touched, grateful, or whining playfully, for example asking a friend to buy you a snack.

intro: ㅇㅇ (eung eung) is a quick texting way to say "yeah" or "yep" in Korean. It is short for 응 (eung), the casual word for "yes".
literal: ㅇ is the consonant used in 응. Typing just the consonants, ㅇㅇ, is a lazy, fast version of 응 or 응응.
usage: ㅇㅇ is for friends, siblings and people your age. It is the texting version of a casual "yep", so never send it to a boss, a teacher or anyone you speak politely to. With them, write 네.
Because it is so short, ㅇㅇ can feel a little flat or careless, especially if it is the whole reply. 응응 or 웅 sounds warmer and friendlier, and 응 ㅎㅎ adds a smile.
Some people read ㅇㅇ as 어어 ("uh-huh"), but the meaning is the same: a simple yes.

forms.note: A cute, soft way to type it.
Polite version for people you respect.

examples.context: Friend asks if you are on your way
Your sister reminds you about dinner
Friend asks if you saw the new episode

faq.q: What does oo mean in Korean texting?
faq.a: "oo" is how people type ㅇㅇ on an English keyboard or describe it in English. It means 응, "yeah".

faq.q: Is ㅇㅇ rude?
faq.a: It is not rude between friends, but it is too casual for anyone you speak politely to. It can also feel a bit cold, so many people use 응응 to sound friendlier.

faq.q: What is the opposite of ㅇㅇ?
faq.a: ㄴㄴ, short for 노노 ("no no"), is the casual texting way to say no.

intro: ㅇㅋ (okay) means "OK" in Korean texting. It is short for 오케이 (okei), the Korean spelling of the English word "okay".
literal: ㅇ and ㅋ are the first consonants of 오 and 케 in 오케이. Typing only the consonants makes it a two-key reply.
usage: ㅇㅋ is one of the most common quick replies between friends: agreeing to a plan, confirming a time, or saying "got it". Doubling it as ㅇㅋㅇㅋ sounds a bit more cheerful and willing.
Like most consonant abbreviations, it is only for friends and people your age or younger. To a boss or an older person, write 네, 알겠습니다 instead.
Spoken versions also exist. 오키 and 오키오키 are cute, casual ways to say okay out loud or in text.

forms.note: Polite version for work or elders.

examples.context: Splitting chores with a roommate
Confirming a meetup time
Friend says they will pick you up

faq.q: How do you say OK in Korean texting?
faq.a: The quickest way is ㅇㅋ. You can also write 오케이, 오키, or ㅇㅋㅇㅋ for a more cheerful tone.

faq.q: Can I send ㅇㅋ to my boss?
faq.a: Better not. It is very casual. Use 네, 알겠습니다 ("Yes, understood") instead.

faq.q: What is the difference between ㅇㅋ and ㅇㅇ?
faq.a: ㅇㅋ is "OK" and is used to agree to something. ㅇㅇ is "yeah" and is used to answer yes to a question. They often overlap.

intro: ㄴㄴ (no no) means "nope" or "no no" in Korean texting. It is short for 노노, the Korean spelling of the English "no no".
literal: ㄴ is the first consonant of 노 (no). Typing it twice is a fast way to write 노노.
usage: Use ㄴㄴ to say no to a question, turn down an offer, or say "no worries, it's fine". For example, ㄴㄴ 괜찮아 is a quick "nah, it's fine".
It sounds light and friendly, not harsh, but it is still very casual. Send it to friends only. For someone you speak politely to, use 아니요.
Like other abbreviations, more letters add emphasis. ㄴㄴㄴㄴ is a strong "no no no", often with a joking or panicked tone.

examples.context: Friend offers to pay you back
Friend asks if you have eaten
Friend guesses the wrong answer

faq.q: What does nn mean in Korean texting?
faq.a: "nn" is ㄴㄴ typed on an English keyboard or written in English letters. It means 노노, "no no" or "nope".

faq.q: Is ㄴㄴ rude?
faq.a: No, it usually sounds light. But it is very casual, so only use it with friends.

faq.q: How do I say yes in the same style?
faq.a: Use ㅇㅇ (from 응, "yeah") or ㅇㅋ ("OK").

intro: ㄱㅅ (gamsa) means "thanks" or "thx" in Korean texting. It is short for 감사 (gamsa), from 감사합니다 ("thank you").
literal: ㄱ and ㅅ are the first consonants of 감 and 사. Some people type the double-consonant letter ㄳ, which is the same two sounds squeezed into one key.
usage: It is funny but true: 감사합니다 is one of the most polite ways to say thank you, yet ㄱㅅ is very casual. Shortening it this much turns it into a quick "thx" between friends, classmates or online strangers.
Do not send ㄱㅅ to a boss, teacher or older person. It can look lazy, as if you could not be bothered to type the full word. Write 감사합니다 or 고맙습니다 instead.
ㄱㅅㄱㅅ ("thanks thanks") sounds a little more cheerful. In online communities, ㄱㅅ is also a common short reply when someone shares information.

forms.note: Same thing, typed as one letter.
Normal casual way to say thanks.

examples.context: Friend lends you a charger
Classmate sends you the lecture notes
Friend says they will save you a seat

faq.q: What does gs mean in Korean texting?
faq.a: "gs" is ㄱㅅ written in English letters. It stands for 감사, "thanks".

faq.q: Is ㄱㅅ polite because it comes from 감사합니다?
faq.a: No. Even though 감사합니다 is polite, shortening it to ㄱㅅ makes it very casual. Use it only with friends.

faq.q: What is ㄳ?
faq.a: ㄳ is a single Korean letter made of ㄱ and ㅅ together. It means the same as ㄱㅅ.

intro: ㅈㅅ (joesong) means "sorry" or "sry" in Korean texting. It is short for 죄송 (joesong), from 죄송합니다 ("I'm sorry").
literal: ㅈ and ㅅ are the first consonants of 죄 and 송. The full phrase 죄송합니다 is a polite, formal apology.
usage: ㅈㅅ is a quick, light apology for small things: being a few minutes late, a typo, or replying slowly. ㅈㅅㅈㅅ ("sorry sorry") is similar and a bit playful.

Because it is so short, it does not feel sincere. Never use it for a real apology or with someone older, your boss or a teacher. That can make things worse. Write 죄송합니다, or 미안해 to a friend you have truly upset.
Like ㄱㅅ, it comes from a polite word, but the abbreviation itself is casual and only for friends or online chats.

examples.context: Arriving a few minutes late to meet a friend
Replying to a message hours later
examples.en: Sorry sorry, just saw it now.

examples.context: Admitting you booked the wrong time

faq.q: What does js mean in Korean texting?
faq.a: "js" is ㅈㅅ written in English letters. It stands for 죄송, "sorry".

faq.q: Is ㅈㅅ a real apology?
faq.a: Only for tiny things between friends. For anything serious, or for anyone older or senior, write out 죄송합니다 or say 미안해 properly.

faq.q: Can ㅈㅅ mean something else?
faq.a: Context usually makes it clear. In a chat where someone made a small mistake, ㅈㅅ almost always means sorry.

intro: ㅊㅋ (chukka) means "congrats" in Korean texting. It is short for 축하 (chukha), from 축하해 ("congratulations").
literal: ㅊ and ㅋ are the first consonants of 축 and 하. The ㅋ comes from how 축하 is pronounced, which sounds like "chu-ka".
usage: ㅊㅋ is a quick, happy way to congratulate a friend on a birthday, a new job, passing a test or anything good. It is almost always doubled as ㅊㅋㅊㅋ, which sounds more excited and warm.

It is casual, so use it with friends, siblings and people your age. For a boss or an older relative, write 축하드려요 or 축하합니다 in full. A real milestone also deserves more than ㅊㅋ, so many people add a longer message after it.
You can put what you are celebrating in front: 생일 ㅊㅋ ("happy birthday"), 합격 ㅊㅋ ("congrats on passing").

examples.context: Friend passes their exam
Group chat on a friend's birthday
Friend gets the job they wanted

faq.q: What does ㅊㅋㅊㅋ mean?
faq.a: ㅊㅋㅊㅋ is 축하축하, an excited "congrats, congrats!". It is the most common way to type it.

faq.q: Can I write ㅊㅋ to my teacher?
faq.a: No, it is too casual. Write 축하드려요 or 축하합니다 instead.

faq.q: Why is it ㅊㅋ and not ㅊㅎ?
faq.a: 축하 is pronounced like "chu-ka", so people type the sound they hear, ㅋ, rather than the spelling.

intro: ㄹㅇ (real) means "for real" or "seriously" in Korean texting. It is short for 리얼 (rieol), the English word "real" written in Korean.
literal: ㄹ and ㅇ are the first consonants of 리 and 얼. The phrase ㄹㅇ루 comes from 리얼로, "for real".
usage: Use ㄹㅇ to stress that something is true, or to agree strongly with a friend. It works a lot like 진짜 ("really"), only more slangy. On its own, ㄹㅇ as a reply means "so true".
ㄹㅇ루 is a fun, extra-slangy way to say "seriously" or "for real", popular with younger people. You will also see 레알, another playful spelling of "real".
This is youth and internet slang. Use it with friends only, never with a boss, teacher or older relative. In speech or polite text, 진짜 or 정말 is the normal word.

examples.context: Eating at a restaurant a friend recommended
Agreeing with a friend's opinion
Complaining after a long day

faq.q: What does rl mean in Korean texting?
faq.a: "rl" is ㄹㅇ written in English letters. It stands for 리얼, "real", and means "for real" or "seriously".

faq.q: What does ㄹㅇ루 mean?
faq.a: It comes from 리얼로, "for real". It is just a slangier way of saying "seriously".

faq.q: Is ㄹㅇ the same as 진짜?
faq.a: They mean almost the same thing. 진짜 is a normal word anyone can say, while ㄹㅇ is texting slang for friends.

intro: ㅇㅈ (injeong) means "agreed", "fair" or "I admit it" in Korean texting. It is short for 인정 (injeong), which means "acknowledgment" or "admitting something is true".
literal: ㅇ and ㅈ are the first consonants of 인 and 정. In standard Korean, 인정하다 means "to admit" or "to recognize".
usage: Friends send ㅇㅈ to agree with something or to admit someone has a point, like "facts" or "fair enough" in English. ㄹㅇ ㅇㅈ means "so true, totally agree".
You will also see it as a question, ㅇㅈ? ("Agree?" / "Right?"), and the playful reply ㅇ ㅇㅈ, short for 어 인정 ("yeah, agreed").
Typed ㅇㅈ is for friends only. The full word 인정 is also common spoken slang among young people, and the polite verb 인정합니다 is perfectly normal at work.

forms.note: The full word, also said out loud.

forms.en: I admit it / I acknowledge it

examples.context: Friend says something that is undeniably true
Joking back and forth in a group chat
Admitting your friend looks great today
examples.en: Gotta admit, you look cool today.

faq.q: What does ij mean in Korean texting?
faq.a: "ij" is ㅇㅈ written in English letters. It stands for 인정, meaning "agreed" or "fair enough".

faq.q: What does ㅇㅈ? ㅇ ㅇㅈ mean?
faq.a: It is a playful exchange: "Agree?" "Yeah, agree." It comes from 인정? 어 인정.

faq.q: Is 인정 slang?
faq.a: 인정 is a normal Korean word meaning "acknowledgment". Using it alone to mean "agreed" or "fair" is casual slang.

intro: ㅂㅂ (bai bai) means "bye bye" in Korean texting. It is short for 바이바이, the English "bye bye" written in Korean.
literal: ㅂ is the first consonant of 바 in 바이. Two ㅂ stand for the two "bye"s.
usage: ㅂㅂ is a quick, light way to end a chat with a friend, like "bb" or "bye". It is cheerful and casual.
Use it only with friends, siblings or people your age. With older people or at work, end with 안녕히 계세요, 들어가세요, or simply 내일 뵙겠습니다 ("see you tomorrow").
You may also see ㅃㅇ, short for 빠이, another playful spelling of "bye".

examples.context: Ending a chat with a friend
Signing off late at night
examples.en: I'm going to sleep now, bye.

examples.context: Wrapping up plans quickly

faq.q: What does bb mean in Korean texting?
faq.a: "bb" is ㅂㅂ written in English letters. It stands for 바이바이, "bye bye".

faq.q: Can I say ㅂㅂ to my teacher?
faq.a: No, it is too casual. Use a polite goodbye such as 안녕히 계세요.

faq.q: Do Koreans say bye bye out loud?
faq.a: Yes, 바이바이 or 빠이 is a common, cute way to say bye among friends, especially young people.

intro: ㄷㄷ (deol deol) means "whoa" or "yikes" in Korean texting, used when something is shocking, scary or impressive. It is short for 덜덜 (deoldeol), the sound of shaking or trembling.
literal: ㄷ is the first consonant of 덜. 덜덜 is an onomatopoeia for trembling, as in 덜덜 떨다 ("to shake all over"), so ㄷㄷ is like saying "I'm shaking".
usage: Use ㄷㄷ when you are shocked: a huge price, a scary story, a crazy score, or a really impressive skill. It can be a scared "yikes" or an amazed "whoa", depending on context.
More ㄷ means a stronger reaction. ㄷㄷㄷ is very common, and ㅎㄷㄷ, from 후덜덜, is an even bigger "I'm trembling".
It is internet slang for friends and online comments. Do not use it with people you speak politely to. Out loud, people say 헐, 와 or 대박 instead.

examples.context: Seeing the price tag on a luxury bag
Friend shares a creepy story
Friend posts an amazing game score

faq.q: What does dd mean in Korean texting?
faq.a: "dd" is ㄷㄷ written in English letters. It comes from 덜덜, the sound of trembling, and means "whoa" or "yikes".

faq.q: Is ㄷㄷ good or bad?
faq.a: Both. It shows shock, which can be fear or amazement. Context tells you which.

faq.q: What is ㅎㄷㄷ?
faq.a: ㅎㄷㄷ is short for 후덜덜, an even stronger "I'm trembling". It is used for very shocking or impressive things.

intro: ㄱㄱ (go go) means "let's go" or "go go" in Korean texting. It is short for 고고, the English "go go" written in Korean.
literal: ㄱ is the first consonant of 고 (go). Two ㄱ stand for 고고.
usage: Friends use ㄱㄱ to suggest a plan or agree to one: 밥 ㄱㄱ? ("wanna go eat?") and the answer ㄱㄱ ("let's go!"). Gamers use it to mean "start" or "let's go".
As a question, ㄱㄱ? means "go?" or "shall we?". ㄱㄱㄱ adds extra excitement and urgency. Be careful not to confuse it with English "gg" ("good game"); in Korean chat, ㄱㄱ means "go".
It is casual and playful, for friends only. With older people, use 가시죠 or 같이 가요 instead.

examples.context: Ready to leave for a meetup
Suggesting lunch to a friend
Planning a night out with friends

faq.q: What does gg mean in Korean texting?
faq.a: When someone writes ㄱㄱ, often spelled "gg" in English letters, it means 고고, "let's go". It is not the gaming "good game".

faq.q: How do I reply to 밥 ㄱㄱ?
faq.a: Say ㄱㄱ or ㅇㅋ to agree, or ㄴㄴ if you cannot go.

faq.q: Is ㄱㄱ polite?
faq.a: No, it is casual slang. Use it only with friends.
